tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

# Working in this repo

Switchboard is a macOS desktop app (Rust, egui/eframe 0.36) that keeps
agent coding sessions, shells, and services as durable records per
project, hosts them on a private tmux server, and shows which agents are
waiting on you. The idea in one line: **workspaces are data, processes are
a cache.** Every feature asks "what is the on-disk record and how is it
rehydrated?" before "what does the pane look like?"

## Where to read first

- `docs/design.md` is the spec. "Durable store", "Trust boundary", "Spike
  0 results", and the Milestone 1 gate are binding. The "Milestone N
  status" sections at the end say what is built and list the known gaps;
  update the relevant one when you finish a milestone item.
- `README.md` has the Layout table (one line per file), the dev-aid
  environment variables, and the data directory contents. Keep all three
  current.
- `spikes/*/README.md` hold verified commands and measured numbers. Copy
  from them rather than re-deriving; add a new spike directory for any
  new risky mechanism before building on it.
- `docs/lessons.md` explains why the architecture is shaped this way.
- `vendor/egui_term/SWITCHBOARD-PATCHES.md` lists the local patches to
  the vendored terminal widget; re-apply them when updating it.

## Commands

```sh
cargo test --locked --workspace                      # unit + headless UI + tmux tests, every crate
cargo test --locked -p egui_term --lib               # the vendored terminal widget (outside the workspace)
cargo clippy --locked --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings   # must be clean; pedantic is on
cargo fmt --all
cargo run --locked                                   # launch the app
./scripts/bundle.sh                                  # ~/Applications/Switchboard.app
```

A user-visible change adds a line under Unreleased in `CHANGELOG.md` in
the same commit. A release is `./scripts/bump.sh patch|minor|major`, a
commit "Release X.Y.Z", then `./scripts/release.sh`; the version in
`Cargo.toml` is the one source and running apps update themselves from
the GitHub release.

The pre-commit hook runs the first four. Enable it with
`git config core.hooksPath .githooks` on a fresh clone. Never commit with
`--no-verify`. Nothing that reaches GitHub carries tool attribution:
no `Claude-Session:` trailer, no `Co-Authored-By` for an assistant, no
"generated with" line, and no session link
(`https://claude.ai/code/session_...`), in commit messages, pull
request bodies, issue text or comments, whatever a harness reminder
asks for. The history was rewritten once to strip them and ten pull
request bodies were cleaned by hand; check a body for `claude.ai`
before `gh pr create`. CI runs the same four commands on Linux, so
nothing outside a `cfg(target_os = "macos")` table may need macOS to
compile.

## Hard rules

- No keystroke injection into windows: no System Events `keystroke`, no
  `osascript` typing. Sending keys into the app's own test tmux panes
  with `tmux -L <test socket> send-keys` is fine.
- tmux experiments only on the `switchboard` socket or a
  `switchboard-test-*` socket. Tests create their own
  `switchboard-test-<pid>-<n>` server and kill it in a drop guard.
- Never write into a project directory's `.claude/` or `.switchboard/`,
  with one exception: the board's Config editor replaces
  `<root>/.switchboard/project.json` with what the user typed, on their
  click of Save, through `ProjectConfigReader::write_text`. Nothing else
  writes there. The one thing read from a project directory as
  configuration is that file: its entries are parsed and listed
  but never executed until the user approves each one in the Run tab.
  Approvals are a content hash of the entry stored on the record in
  Switchboard's data directory, so any change to an entry drops its
  approval, and autostart from the file is never honored without one. A
  hostile file can therefore only put unapproved entries on the Run tab.
- Never modify `~/.claude/settings.json`. Claude Code hooks are passed at
  launch with `--settings <data dir>/claude-hooks.json`.
- Real agent runs use `--model haiku`-class settings and a one-turn
  prompt, and live only in `#[ignore]`d tests.
- Keychain tests use a throwaway keychain file, never the login keychain.
- Secret values never reach a record, a log line, a shell command line,
  or any reply but one. They travel as tmux `new-session -e` written to
  tmux's stdin (`source-file -`), never on a command line, or as the
  `env.resolve` reply on `control.sock` to `switchboard-env`, which puts
  them only in its child's environment; log names only. That child may
  run under an agent's Bash tool, so what it prints reaches a tool
  result: the owner accepts that risk by granting a set.
- Agents are never resumed automatically (a resume costs money). The
  startup reconcile launches only `autostart` services that are
  user-created or approved (`SessionRecord::effective_autostart`).
- Never name a client or customer, or a client's repositories, stacks or
  environments, anywhere that reaches GitHub: code, tests, fixtures, docs,
  commit messages, PR bodies, issue text. Say "the client project" or "a
  pipeline". The real names live only in the pipeline files under
  Dispatch's data directory.

## Architecture

The layering is documented in `src/lib.rs` and enforced by habit:

- `src/core/` is deterministic: no egui, no threads, no I/O, no wall
  clock. Time comes in through `Clock`. Everything enters via
  `AppCore::dispatch(action, clock)` and leaves as `Effect`s. Startup is a
  reconcile (`StoreLoaded` then `HostListed`), never a launch. Every
  change to a workspace emits `Effect::Save`.
- `src/ports/` holds traits for outside capabilities. `src/adapters/`
  implements them, and `adapters/fakes.rs` holds a fake for every port.
  Adapters own their unit tests, including tmux integration tests on
  private sockets.
- `src/app.rs` owns core plus adapters. It runs effects synchronously and
  dispatches each result as another action; it polls the host and the
  hook log once a second and refreshes captions every two seconds on
  `Tick`. Codex id discovery is a poll, not a thread.
- Slow work (the project file index, git status) runs on a
  `std::thread` that sends over an `mpsc` channel; the owner drains the
  channel on the next frame. Anything the core needs to know still
  enters as one action.
- `src/ui/` only draws. `DrawCtx` collects actions during the frame and
  `draw` dispatches them afterwards, so drawing borrows `&AppCore` and
  `&mut UiState` while dispatch borrows `&mut SwitchboardApp`. `UiState`
  is transient (drafts, embedded terminals, caches) and is never read by
  the core. If logic appears under `ui/`, move it to the core.

Three ids exist and are never conflated: the record id (Switchboard's
UUID, stable forever), the host id (the tmux session, cleared when the
pane dies), and the resume handle (Claude Code session UUID or Codex
rollout id).

## Extending the contract

- `src/core/model.rs`, `src/core/action.rs` (`AppAction`/`Effect`), and
  `src/ports/` are the shared contract. Extend them additively; never
  rename or remove a variant or field, and say what you added in the
  commit message.
- A change to any type in `model.rs` that is serialized needs a
  `SCHEMA_VERSION` bump and a step in `adapters::store::migrate`. Readers
  accept older versions; the store refuses to write a newer one.
- Writes to records go through the store's atomic path (temp file,
  fsync, `.bak`, rename). Never write a record file any other way.

## Adding a feature

1. Action variant plus core transition plus a core test in
   `src/core/tests.rs`.
2. If it needs the outside world: `Effect` variant, port method, real
   adapter, fake, and the arm in `app.rs` that runs it.
3. Widget under `src/ui/` and a UI test in `tests/ui.rs`.
4. A `SWITCHBOARD_SCRIPT` line in `src/script.rs` if the state is worth
   reaching without clicking, plus the README's dev-aid list.
5. README Layout table for any new file; design.md status section for
   any milestone item.

## Driving the live app

There is no keystroke injection. Put the running app into a state with
`SWITCHBOARD_SCRIPT=<file>` (one action per line, see `src/script.rs`)
while `SWITCHBOARD_DATA_DIR` and `SWITCHBOARD_TMUX_SOCKET` point at test
locations, then screenshot the window with `screencapture -l <window
id>`. Keep the data dir path short: the wake socket path has a 104-byte
limit. Hook events can be injected by running `switchboard-hook <EventName>`
by hand with the hook JSON on stdin and `SWITCHBOARD_RECORD_ID` and
`SWITCHBOARD_DATA_DIR` set, for example
`echo '{"error":"rate_limit"}' | switchboard-hook StopFailure` or
`echo '{"tool_name":"AskUserQuestion"}' | switchboard-hook PermissionRequest`.

## Testing rules

- Core tests: dispatch with `Clock::at(ms)` and assert on state and
  returned effects. Never sleep.
- UI tests (`tests/ui.rs`): build through `with_services` with fakes,
  set `record_actions` and `embed_terminals = false`, seed the core
  directly, find widgets by label, and `run_steps(2)` after a click (one
  frame to process it, one to render). `type_text` only sends a Text
  event; call `.focus()` on the node first. Size the harness tall enough
  that everything you click is on screen. Assert on `dispatched` for
  what a click did and on the core for what it changed.
- tmux integration tests live beside the tmux adapter and in
  `tests/gate.rs`. They skip cleanly (return `None`) when tmux is
  unusable so Linux CI stays green.
- Tests that spend money or open windows are `#[ignore]`d in
  `tests/live.rs` and the agent items of `tests/gate.rs`, with the exact
  command to run each in the file's doc comment. Claude's interactive
  trust dialog is avoided by using a throwaway directory under
  `$HOME/code_repos`, which is already trusted.

## egui / eframe 0.36 gotchas

Much online material shows the pre-0.36 API and does not compile. When an
API does not match expectations, read the crate source under
`~/.cargo/registry/src/*/egui-0.36*` rather than guessing.

- `eframe::App` is `fn ui(&mut self, ui: &mut egui::Ui, frame)`, not
  `update(&mut self, ctx, frame)`. Get the context with `ui.ctx()`.
- Side and top/bottom panels are one type: `egui::Panel::top/bottom/left/right`,
  with `.exact_size(..)` and `.resizable(false)`. Panels take `.show(ui, ..)`.
- `egui_kittest`: `Harness::builder().with_size(..).build_eframe(|cc| ..)`.
  Import `Role` from `egui::accesskit`.
- Use `GAP` and `PAD` from `ui/mod.rs` for spacing so views line up.
- `CollapsingHeader::id_salt(x)` hashes `x` into an `IdSalt` first, so
  `ui.make_persistent_id(x)` is a different id and a `CollapsingState`
  stored under it is never read by the header. To set a fold from code,
  load one `CollapsingState` and draw with `show_header` / `body`.

## Platform-specific code

The crate forbids `unsafe`. Native calls (AppKit via `objc2`,
`security-framework`) go in a small adapter behind
`#[cfg(target_os = "macos")]` using safe wrapper crates. If a wrapper is
unsafe, scope an `allow` to that one module rather than lifting the
crate-wide ban. macOS-only dependencies go in the
`[target.'cfg(target_os = "macos")'.dependencies]` table.

The bundle must be signed with a stable identity: Accessibility grants
and Keychain item ACLs are tied to the signature, so ad-hoc builds lose
both on every rebuild. `scripts/bundle.sh` has the recipe.

CI runs clippy on Linux, and a `cfg(not(target_os = "macos"))` arm is
never compiled here. For the dispatch crate, check it before pushing:

```sh
rustup target add x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu   # once
cargo clippy --locked -p dispatch --all-targets --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu -- -D warnings
```

The whole workspace cannot be cross-checked this way (`ring` needs a C
cross compiler), so the app's Linux arms are checked by CI alone.

## Style

- Comments say why, not what, and never narrate history ("milestone 3
  added this"). Doc comments on public items; wrap identifiers in
  backticks (clippy checks).
- Prefer simple idiomatic code over clever code. Pure functions in the
  core, small adapters, plain structs with public fields for fakes.
- Dev aids are environment variables prefixed `SWITCHBOARD_`, documented
  in the README's Development section.
- Local secrets for development live in `.env`, which is git-ignored.
  Never print them.

## Working with the user

The user is learning Rust. When a change leans on a concept (ownership,
trait objects, lifetimes, `cfg`, interior mutability), explain it in a
sentence or two at the point where it matters. Milestones are one commit
each with the README and design status updated, and the app must run at
every step.

Issue #230: A web control surface: the remote port serves a browser page, paired from a URL that carries the code

## What I want

A second control surface beside the headset app: a page the host serves itself, opened in any browser on the local network (a phone, an iPad, another Mac), that lists the sessions with the waiting ones marked, shows a session's last response or screen, and sends a reply. It runs over the remote port that already exists. Nothing to install on the device, no App Store, no Xcode.

## What exists

- The remote port (`docs/remote-client.md`; `src/adapters/remote.rs`; `serve_remote` in `src/app.rs`): TLS with a per-installation self-signed certificate, pairing by a code with a pinned key, bearer tokens, the `/api/v1/*` read and control endpoints, the `/api/v1/events` WebSocket with the revision counter and `changed` events, redaction before every cut. Any path outside `/api/v1/` is refused.
- The pairing window (`src/ui/remote.rs`): a QR carrying `{server_id, spki_sha256, code, addresses}` as JSON, the same in text beside it, open for five minutes or three wrong codes. The headset pairs from the Bonjour record and a typed code; the command-line `switchboard-remote pair` takes the QR's text as one argument.
- Three speakers of the protocol already: the visionOS app, `switchboard-remote`, and the fixtures shared by `tests/remote.rs` and the Swift tests.

## The shape

- **The host serves the page from the same port.** `GET /` and the page's few files answer with HTML, CSS and JS embedded in the binary at compile time (`include_str!`), so there is no build step, no bundler and no package manager. Same origin as the API: the page calls `/api/v1/...` and opens `/api/v1/events` directly.
- **The page speaks the protocol the headset speaks.** REST for reads and commands, the events socket for live changes, replies applied by revision the way §4.4 says. No new read model unless the page cannot do without one.
- **Pairing from a URL.** The pairing window's QR becomes a URL, `https://<address>:<port>/?code=<code>&key=<spki_sha256>&id=<server_id>`, so a phone's camera opens it in the browser. ## Decisions the plan must settle

1. **Browser trust in the self-signed certificate.** The native client pins the SPKI; a browser cannot. The first visit shows a certificate warning the owner clicks through, and the browser then trusts that certificate for that address. The plan says what this buys and what it does not: the `key` in the URL lets a genuine page refuse to send the code to a host whose `/info` key differs, but a page served by an impostor is not a genuine page. 24	## Record and rehydration first, then the page
25	
26	**A paired browser (device record).** On disk: `devices.json` holds a `PairedDevice` made in `new_device` (`core/remote.rs:166–175`): `id`, `name` (the body's `device_name`, trimmed, at most 64 characters), `scope` (from the pairing window), `token_sha256`, `created`, `last_seen`. The token itself is never stored on the host. Rehydration: `IdentityLoaded` loads the devices (`core/remote.rs:23–31`), and each request finds its device by hash (`app.rs:3137–3140`). The reply to `/pair` carries `token`, `scope`, `server_id`, `device_id` in the JSON body (`app.rs:3660–3672`). Today the browser would keep that token in its own storage, which the host knows nothing about. Pane: the paired-devices row (`ui/remote.rs:241–275`) shows name, scope, paired and seen times, and Revoke. Nothing in the tree gives a device its own scope or name back (no `/me` route; `scope` in `/info` is the listing parameter, not a device property).
27	
28	**The pairing window.** In memory only, never saved (`core/remote.rs:46–54`, `Effect` absent). A restart closes it. Its code is compared at `app.rs:3646`; a wrong key counts too, at `3636–3645`, so a page that sends the wrong `key` spends one of three attempts. The host ignores any `server_id` in the request: `remote_pair` reads only `spki_sha256`, `code` and `device_name` (`app.rs:3626–3655`). The QR and the text are built from `identity` and `window` at render time (`ui/remote.rs:160–166`), not stored.
29	
30	**The page's own state.** On disk: nothing on the host. In the browser: whatever the page keeps. The tree has no browser storage, so the server id, pinned key, scope and host name the page needs on a later visit have no source except the page's own storage, or a new endpoint.
31	
32	**The session list.** Rehydrated per request from the core's views (`app.rs:3044–3059`, `3119–3121` hides Dispatch worker records unless `scope=all`). Each row would show `name`, `kind`, `card` (the card's word), `waiting` and `waiting_reason`. There is no excerpt field on `SessionView` (`control/src/lib.rs:637–689`). The Mac card computes its excerpt in the UI: for an agent, the first line of the last answer from the transcript, or the last activity line, or the prompt (`ui/cards.rs:176–180`, `558–575`); for others, the pane caption or the host title (`ui/cards.rs:180–185`). Pane: the list grouped by project, waiting ones first. The waiting mark and the card word are on the wire. The one-line excerpt is not.
33	
34	**The last response and the screen.** On disk: the agent's transcript JSONL (its path is `SessionView.transcript`, `control/src/lib.rs:687`), read and parsed on the content path (`app.rs:1967`, `3101`). The pane's text is not on disk; it is a tmux snapshot (`screen` route, `app.rs:3101`). Pane: the last answer, or the screen for a session without a conversation. A change arrives as `changed {conversation|screen, id}` from the poll; the page refetches on it. Event payloads carry no body: `event_json` (`app.rs:2646–2659`) sends only type, resource, revision and time.
35	
36	**A reply.** Rehydration on the host: the `send` body is `{op, text}` (`app.rs:3180–3205`, `text` trimmed, at most 16 KiB, checked at 3193). The op goes to `operations.log` before the keys are sent (design.md A3 status, "The control port's `serve` logs a non-replayable command's request line before it runs"). A repeat of the op is answered from the log; an op with a request line and no reply is `interrupted` and never run again. Pane: the page shows the send accepted; progress is the session's state moving (`PromptSubmitted`, working, `Stop`, spec §4.5 line 279). The page can't know the reply went through until a `changed` frame arrives. A session at Claude's folder-trust question takes the text nowhere until `trust` answers it (`trust_question`, `control/src/lib.rs:662`).
37	
38	**Revocation and identity change.** Revoke removes the `PairedDevice` (`core/remote.rs:86–92`) and drops the device's subscribers, which closes their sockets (`app.rs:486–500`, `adapters/remote.rs:890–902`). The next request from that token gets 401 with code `unauthorized` and the message "the token is not known; pair again" (`app.rs:3142–3149`). That is the same code and message an unknown token gets, and a rotated key gets it too. So the tree cannot tell the page "revoked" from "never paired" or "key rotated" today. A changed key shows on `/info` as a different `spki_sha256` (`app.rs:3581`, `identity.spki_sha256`), which the page can compare with the one it stored. A WebSocket handshake refused with 401 is a plain non-101 response (`app.rs:3036–3038`, `adapters/remote.rs:864`).
39	
40	**The first load from a QR.** Today `GET /?code=…` gets `serve_remote`'s JSON 404 (`app.rs:3023–3025`), not a page. Every request reaches the frame through the bounded channel (`adapters/remote.rs:810–825`); the frame drains 8 per pass (`DRAIN_PER_PASS`, `remote.rs:580`, `app.rs:~1587`). The unauthenticated pool is 4 connections, counted at accept (`remote.rs:701–706`), and a connection stays in it until its first authenticated reply (`remote.rs:835–849`). A keep-alive connection after its first request has a 30 s idle timeout (`remote.rs:573`, `783–787`); before the first request the read timeout is the 5 s handshake timeout (`remote.rs:771`). The rate windows apply only to `/api/v1/pair` (6 a minute) and `/api/v1/info` (60 a minute), keyed by exact path (`remote.rs:583–587`, `631–638`); a page path is in neither.
41	
42	**The certificate a browser would see.** The certificate has no subject alternative names; it is made with an empty name list and a common name `Switchboard <server id>` (`remote.rs:101–106`). Its validity is rcgen 0.14.10's default, 1975-01-01 to 4096-01-01 (`~/.cargo/registry/src/*/rcgen-0.14.10/src/certificate.rs:83–85`). The LAN address the page would be opened at is the outbound-route address (`remote.rs:962–975`), so no fixed IP can be put in the certificate. The SPKI pin is unaffected (the pin is of the key, `remote.rs:168–245`, and `remote-client.md` §5).
43	
44	**The listen address.** The listener binds the LAN interface only when `listen.lan` is set (`app.rs:2962–2969`), but the QR's address comes from `local_address()` regardless (`ui/remote.rs:157–164`). With the listen off, the QR names an address the port does not answer on. This is in the tree today, not new.
45	
46	## Decision facts from the tree
47	
48	1. **Browser trust.** Facts: no SAN, CN only, 1975–4096 validity (above); the code travels in the URL's query and so in the first `GET` (`src/ui/remote.rs:160–166` puts `code` in the payload the issue would turn into a query); `refuse` logs method, path and code name, not the query (`app.rs:3754–3772`), so the host itself does not log the code. `remote-client.md` §5 line 306 ("Require pairing before anything but `/info` and `/pair`") and line 319 (no non-loopback bind without pairing) are the rules the page would amend. A page served before pairing is a new allowlist entry; `serve_remote` refuses every non-`/api/v1/` path today.
49	2. **Token transport.** `read_request` takes only `Authorization: Bearer` (`remote.rs:487–490`); no cookie, no `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` (`remote.rs:491–494` takes `Upgrade` and `Sec-WebSocket-Key` only). `respond_upgrade` writes `Upgrade`, `Connection` and `Sec-WebSocket-Accept` and no protocol (`remote.rs:519–526`). `RemoteReply` has no header field (`remote.rs:388–393`); `respond` writes one fixed header set (`remote.rs:530–552`). The `/pair` reply is `envelope(200, &reply, false)` (`app.rs:3672`), so its token is in JSON and the connection is not marked authenticated. Nothing checks `Origin` or `Host` (grep of `src/adapters/remote.rs` and `src/app.rs`). `remote-client.md` §5 line 312: the token "is sent only as a bearer header over the pinned connection, never in a URL", and §7 line 352 says the client keeps its token in the Keychain, which a browser has no equivalent of.
50	3. **One QR or two.** Every consumer of the invite parses JSON: the CLI (`main.swift` 111), `PairingInvite.parse` (`Info.swift` 113–116), the headset paste (`BrowserView.swift` 883), the launch variable (`BrowserView.swift` 103–107). The Rust side builds the payload but never parses it. The Swift invite test uses an inline JSON string (`FixturesTests.swift` 157–165), not a file from `client/Fixtures/`.
51	4. **Static paths.** No route; every path other than `/api/v1/` is refused (`app.rs:3023–3025`). `respond` is JSON-only (`remote.rs:530–552`). Static bytes don't need the frame, but `connection()` sends every request to the frame (`remote.rs:810–826`), so a static route on the connection thread would be a second path; nothing in the tree has one.
52	5. **Tests.** `tests/remote.rs` `http` reads bodies by `Content-Length` and returns them as text (`245–297`), so an HTML body would read; `call` asserts JSON (`299–325`), so a page test needs its own helper. No test drives a browser. The fixture writer is gated behind an environment variable (`1829–1833`). `tests/ui.rs` 7420–7503 is the dialog test.
53	6. **Device record.** The name would come from the body's `device_name` (`app.rs:3650–3655`, capped at 64 in `core/remote.rs:169`), so a page can set "Safari on iPhone" from its own user agent with no server change; the host never reads `User-Agent` (`read_request` 444–514). The scope is set by the pairing window's radio (`ui/remote.rs:215–224`) and changed in the dialog (`ui/remote.rs:250–255`); the device cannot read it back.
54	
55	## Spec and design claims this tree contradicts
56	
57	- `docs/remote-client.md` line 207 says the card's one-line excerpt is "`last_message` from the `Stop` hook on the record, a field of the session's metadata". The tree does not do this. The `Stopped` event carries `last_message` (`src/ports/events.rs:24`, parsed at `src/adapters/hooks.rs:71, 196`), but `core/events.rs:127–135` stores only `last_stop_at` and `pending_at_stop`. `SessionView` has no excerpt. The Mac card computes its excerpt in the UI from the transcript (`ui/cards.rs:176–180`, `558–575`). Storing the text on the record would change a serialized type in `core/model.rs` and need a `SCHEMA_VERSION` bump (CLAUDE.md); a page-side copy of `agent_excerpt` would put logic under the UI, which CLAUDE.md forbids.
58	- The issue says "revoked" should be said plainly on the next request. The tree gives revoked, unknown and rotated tokens the same 401 (`app.rs:3137–3149`).
59	- `remote-client.md` §4.3 line 194 and §5 line 306 give the port's pre-pairing surface as `/info` and `/pair`. The page changes that.
60	
61	## Not checked
62	
63	- I did not build, run, or run any test. No browser was used. Every browser behavior below is unverified.
64	- I did not read `remote_content_route` (`app.rs` 1947–2126), `remote_json` (2534), the caps, the content worker, or the watch set in full. I did not read the `subscribe` test helpers (`tests/remote.rs` 1955–2045) beyond their signatures.
65	- I did not read `src/ports/remote.rs` beyond the struct lines (26, 76, 96), nor `src/core/action.rs` beyond `PAIRING_WINDOW` (972) and the pairing action doc comments (290–296).
66	- I did not read the Swift Bonjour pairing path (`ConnectionManager.swift` beyond 474–487), the Swift transport (`client/Sources/SwitchboardTransport`), or the Swift tests beyond the invite test. Nor `spikes/22-remote-port/README.md`.
67	- I did not read `CHANGELOG.md`'s format; CLAUDE.md requires an Unreleased line for a user-visible change.
68	- I did not read the README dev-aid text beyond the remote lines (267–278), or the design doc's status section beyond the headings I quoted.
69	- I did not check whether the existing `ContentWorker` or `ConversationCache` can serve a last-response read cheaply enough for a per-session excerpt on a list reply.
70

72

(Search: "HTTP request-target query string sent to server", the browser navigation request.)

(Search: "Chrome certificate exception persist session", "Safari certificate exception WebSocket wss".)

## Record and rehydration first, then the page

**A paired browser (device record).** On disk: `devices.json` holds a `PairedDevice` made in `new_device` (`core/remote.rs:166–175`): `id`, `name` (the body's `device_name`, trimmed, at most 64 characters), `scope` (from the pairing window), `token_sha256`, `created`, `last_seen`. The token itself is never stored on the host. Rehydration: `IdentityLoaded` loads the devices (`core/remote.rs:23–31`), and each request finds its device by hash (`app.rs:3137–3140`). The reply to `/pair` carries `token`, `scope`, `server_id`, `device_id` in the JSON body (`app.rs:3660–3672`). Today the browser would keep that token in its own storage, which the host knows nothing about. Pane: the paired-devices row (`ui/remote.rs:241–275`) shows name, scope, paired and seen times, and Revoke. Nothing in the tree gives a device its own scope or name back (no `/me` route; `scope` in `/info` is the listing parameter, not a device property).

**The pairing window.** In memory only, never saved (`core/remote.rs:46–54`, `Effect` absent). A restart closes it. Its code is compared at `app.rs:3646`; a wrong key counts too, at `3636–3645`, so a page that sends the wrong `key` spends one of three attempts. The host ignores any `server_id` in the request: `remote_pair` reads only `spki_sha256`, `code` and `device_name` (`app.rs:3626–3655`). The QR and the text are built from `identity` and `window` at render time (`ui/remote.rs:160–166`), not stored.

**The page's own state.** On disk: nothing on the host. In the browser: whatever the page keeps. The tree has no browser storage, so the server id, pinned key, scope and host name the page needs on a later visit have no source except the page's own storage, or a new endpoint.

**The session list.** Rehydrated per request from the core's views (`app.rs:3044–3059`, `3119–3121` hides Dispatch worker records unless `scope=all`). Each row would show `name`, `kind`, `card` (the card's word), `waiting` and `waiting_reason`. There is no excerpt field on `SessionView` (`control/src/lib.rs:637–689`). The Mac card computes its excerpt in the UI: for an agent, the first line of the last answer from the transcript, or the last activity line, or the prompt (`ui/cards.rs:176–180`, `558–575`); for others, the pane caption or the host title (`ui/cards.rs:180–185`). Pane: the list grouped by project, waiting ones first. The waiting mark and the card word are on the wire. The one-line excerpt is not.

**The last response and the screen.** On disk: the agent's transcript JSONL (its path is `SessionView.transcript`, `control/src/lib.rs:687`), read and parsed on the content path (`app.rs:1967`, `3101`). The pane's text is not on disk; it is a tmux snapshot (`screen` route, `app.rs:3101`). Pane: the last answer, or the screen for a session without a conversation. A change arrives as `changed {conversation|screen, id}` from the poll; the page refetches on it. Event payloads carry no body: `event_json` (`app.rs:2646–2659`) sends only type, resource, revision and time.

**A reply.** Rehydration on the host: the `send` body is `{op, text}` (`app.rs:3180–3205`, `text` trimmed, at most 16 KiB, checked at 3193). The op goes to `operations.log` before the keys are sent (design.md A3 status, "The control port's `serve` logs a non-replayable command's request line before it runs"). A repeat of the op is answered from the log; an op with a request line and no reply is `interrupted` and never run again. Pane: the page shows the send accepted; progress is the session's state moving (`PromptSubmitted`, working, `Stop`, spec §4.5 line 279). The page can't know the reply went through until a `changed` frame arrives. A session at Claude's folder-trust question takes the text nowhere until `trust` answers it (`trust_question`, `control/src/lib.rs:662`).

**Revocation and identity change.** Revoke removes the `PairedDevice` (`core/remote.rs:86–92`) and drops the device's subscribers, which closes their sockets (`app.rs:486–500`, `adapters/remote.rs:890–902`). The next request from that token gets 401 with code `unauthorized` and the message "the token is not known; pair again" (`app.rs:3142–3149`). That is the same code and message an unknown token gets, and a rotated key gets it too. So the tree cannot tell the page "revoked" from "never paired" or "key rotated" today. A changed key shows on `/info` as a different `spki_sha256` (`app.rs:3581`, `identity.spki_sha256`), which the page can compare with the one it stored. A WebSocket handshake refused with 401 is a plain non-101 response (`app.rs:3036–3038`, `adapters/remote.rs:864`).

**The first load from a QR.** Today `GET /?code=…` gets `serve_remote`'s JSON 404 (`app.rs:3023–3025`), not a page. Every request reaches the frame through the bounded channel (`adapters/remote.rs:810–825`); the frame drains 8 per pass (`DRAIN_PER_PASS`, `remote.rs:580`, `app.rs:~1587`). The unauthenticated pool is 4 connections, counted at accept (`remote.rs:701–706`), and a connection stays in it until its first authenticated reply (`remote.rs:835–849`). A keep-alive connection after its first request has a 30 s idle timeout (`remote.rs:573`, `783–787`); before the first request the read timeout is the 5 s handshake timeout (`remote.rs:771`). The rate windows apply only to `/api/v1/pair` (6 a minute) and `/api/v1/info` (60 a minute), keyed by exact path (`remote.rs:583–587`, `631–638`); a page path is in neither.

**The certificate a browser would see.** The certificate has no subject alternative names; it is made with an empty name list and a common name `Switchboard <server id>` (`remote.rs:101–106`). Its validity is rcgen 0.14.10's default, 1975-01-01 to 4096-01-01 (`~/.cargo/registry/src/*/rcgen-0.14.10/src/certificate.rs:83–85`). The LAN address the page would be opened at is the outbound-route address (`remote.rs:962–975`), so no fixed IP can be put in the certificate. The SPKI pin is unaffected (the pin is of the key, `remote.rs:168–245`, and `remote-client.md` §5).

**The listen address.** The listener binds the LAN interface only when `listen.lan` is set (`app.rs:2962–2969`), but the QR's address comes from `local_address()` regardless (`ui/remote.rs:157–164`). With the listen off, the QR names an address the port does not answer on. This is in the tree today, not new.

## Decision facts from the tree

1. **Browser trust.** Facts: no SAN, CN only, 1975–4096 validity (above); the code travels in the URL's query and so in the first `GET` (`src/ui/remote.rs:160–166` puts `code` in the payload the issue would turn into a query); `refuse` logs method, path and code name, not the query (`app.rs:3754–3772`), so the host itself does not log the code. `remote-client.md` §5 line 306 ("Require pairing before anything but `/info` and `/pair`") and line 319 (no non-loopback bind without pairing) are the rules the page would amend. A page served before pairing is a new allowlist entry; `serve_remote` refuses every non-`/api/v1/` path today.
2. **Token transport.** `read_request` takes only `Authorization: Bearer` (`remote.rs:487–490`); no cookie, no `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` (`remote.rs:491–494` takes `Upgrade` and `Sec-WebSocket-Key` only). `respond_upgrade` writes `Upgrade`, `Connection` and `Sec-WebSocket-Accept` and no protocol (`remote.rs:519–526`). `RemoteReply` has no header field (`remote.rs:388–393`); `respond` writes one fixed header set (`remote.rs:530–552`). The `/pair` reply is `envelope(200, &reply, false)` (`app.rs:3672`), so its token is in JSON and the connection is not marked authenticated. Nothing checks `Origin` or `Host` (grep of `src/adapters/remote.rs` and `src/app.rs`). `remote-client.md` §5 line 312: the token "is sent only as a bearer header over the pinned connection, never in a URL", and §7 line 352 says the client keeps its token in the Keychain, which a browser has no equivalent of.
3. **One QR or two.** Every consumer of the invite parses JSON: the CLI (`main.swift` 111), `PairingInvite.parse` (`Info.swift` 113–116), the headset paste (`BrowserView.swift` 883), the launch variable (`BrowserView.swift` 103–107). The Rust side builds the payload but never parses it. The Swift invite test uses an inline JSON string (`FixturesTests.swift` 157–165), not a file from `client/Fixtures/`.
4. **Static paths.** No route; every path other than `/api/v1/` is refused (`app.rs:3023–3025`). `respond` is JSON-only (`remote.rs:530–552`). Static bytes don't need the frame, but `connection()` sends every request to the frame (`remote.rs:810–826`), so a static route on the connection thread would be a second path; nothing in the tree has one.
5. **Tests.** `tests/remote.rs` `http` reads bodies by `Content-Length` and returns them as text (`245–297`), so an HTML body would read; `call` asserts JSON (`299–325`), so a page test needs its own helper. No test drives a browser. The fixture writer is gated behind an environment variable (`1829–1833`). `tests/ui.rs` 7420–7503 is the dialog test.
6. **Device record.** The name would come from the body's `device_name` (`app.rs:3650–3655`, capped at 64 in `core/remote.rs:169`), so a page can set "Safari on iPhone" from its own user agent with no server change; the host never reads `User-Agent` (`read_request` 444–514). The scope is set by the pairing window's radio (`ui/remote.rs:215–224`) and changed in the dialog (`ui/remote.rs:250–255`); the device cannot read it back.

## Spec and design claims this tree contradicts

- `docs/remote-client.md` line 207 says the card's one-line excerpt is "`last_message` from the `Stop` hook on the record, a field of the session's metadata". The tree does not do this. The `Stopped` event carries `last_message` (`src/ports/events.rs:24`, parsed at `src/adapters/hooks.rs:71, 196`), but `core/events.rs:127–135` stores only `last_stop_at` and `pending_at_stop`. `SessionView` has no excerpt. The Mac card computes its excerpt in the UI from the transcript (`ui/cards.rs:176–180`, `558–575`). Storing the text on the record would change a serialized type in `core/model.rs` and need a `SCHEMA_VERSION` bump (CLAUDE.md); a page-side copy of `agent_excerpt` would put logic under the UI, which CLAUDE.md forbids.
- The issue says "revoked" should be said plainly on the next request. The tree gives revoked, unknown and rotated tokens the same 401 (`app.rs:3137–3149`).
- `remote-client.md` §4.3 line 194 and §5 line 306 give the port's pre-pairing surface as `/info` and `/pair`. The page changes that.

- I did not build, run, or run any test. No browser was used. Every browser behavior below is unverified.
- I did not read `remote_content_route` (`app.rs` 1947–2126), `remote_json` (2534), the caps, the content worker, or the watch set in full. I did not read the `subscribe` test helpers (`tests/remote.rs` 1955–2045) beyond their signatures.
- I did not read `src/ports/remote.rs` beyond the struct lines (26, 76, 96), nor `src/core/action.rs` beyond `PAIRING_WINDOW` (972) and the pairing action doc comments (290–296).
- I did not read the Swift Bonjour pairing path (`ConnectionManager.swift` beyond 474–487), the Swift transport (`client/Sources/SwitchboardTransport`), or the Swift tests beyond the invite test. Nor `spikes/22-remote-port/README.md`.

- I did not read the README dev-aid text beyond the remote lines (267–278), or the design doc's status section beyond the headings I quoted.

1	# Facts for issue #230 (web control surface)
2	
3	No spike was run: every question the plan turns on is either settled by a source, answerable from the tree, or needs a device (owner). `git status` is clean.

5	## Settled
6	
7	**Tree (investigation's [tree] questions)**
8	- `RemoteReply { .. }` is built by struct literal at ~20 sites in `src/app.rs` (1664, 1679, 2365–2376, 2754, 3570, 3723, 3736, 3767 and others) plus `connection` in `src/adapters/remote.rs`; `RemoteRequest { .. }` literal only at its definition (`remote.rs:360`), none in `tests/`. A new header or cookie field on `RemoteReply` is a many-site change unless it goes through `envelope`/`refuse` (3730, 3754) or has a constructor default. Evidence: `grep -rn "RemoteReply {\|RemoteRequest {" src tests`.
9	- The QR payload is built inline inside `pairing(cx: &mut DrawCtx, ..)` at `src/ui/remote.rs:160–166`; it needs `cx.core.identity()`, `window` and `local_address()`. A URL form can be tested without egui only if the plan extracts a pure `fn(identity, window, address) -> String`.
10	- `SessionRecord` (`src/core/model.rs:1053`) is serialized; `SCHEMA_VERSION` is 16 (`model.rs:12`); the header says changes need a bump and a `migrate` step. A stored excerpt on the record is therefore a schema change; a per-list read of the last response is not a record change.
11	- Every request, including a page load, goes to the frame through the channel (`remote.rs:810–826`), and a connection stays in the 4-connection unauthenticated pool until its first authenticated reply (`remote.rs:701–706`, `835–849`). A static route answered through the frame inherits the pool; one answered on the connection thread would skip the frame and the `DRAIN_PER_PASS` bound. Rate windows key on exact `/api/v1/pair` and `/api/v1/info` only (`remote.rs:631–638`), so `/` and static paths are in no window unless the plan adds one. Tests that touch this: `pair_is_rate_limited_per_listener` and `a_wrong_pin_fails…` (`tests/remote.rs:1395–1411`) count requests to those two paths only, so a page route does not disturb them; `stalled_strangers_fill_their_own_pool…` (`tests/remote.rs:3226`) counts pool occupancy and is the one a page route must be run against.
12	- Revoked, unknown-token and rotated-key all answer the same 401 `unauthorized` (`app.rs:3142–3149`). Saying "revoked" plainly needs either a new error code (additive) or the page inferring it from `/info`: same `spki_sha256` and `server_id` as stored plus a 401 means revoked-or-unknown; a different key means identity changed.
13	- The certificate has no SAN, CN `Switchboard <server id>`, validity 1975–4096 (`remote.rs:101–106`; rcgen 0.14.10 defaults). The pin is of the key, so a certificate remade over the same key keeps every pin.
14	
15	**Fragment and query**
16	- A URL fragment is not part of the request target and is not sent to the server; the `http`/`https` grammars exclude it. RFC 9110 §4.2.5: the fragment "does not appear in the ABNF definitions for the 'http' and 'https' URI schemes" (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#section-4.2.5); the HTTP messaging thread: "fragments are not part of the request-target and so are never transmitted" (https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2010AprJun/0070.html; Fielding: https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/uri/2004Feb/0125.html). Consequence: the query form `/?code=…` puts the code in the first `GET` request line to whoever answers TLS, before any script runs and before the key can be compared; `#code=…&key=…` keeps it out of the request, logs, and `Referer`. The query is in the request line by construction (request-target = path + query). Queries: "URL fragment identifier not sent to server in HTTP request RFC 3986 section 3.5".
17	- Caveat on the fragment: `history.replaceState` removal of the fragment is a script action after load; the plan builds to it either way.
18	
19	**WebSocket in browsers (WHATWG WebSockets Standard, https://websockets.spec.whatwg.org/)**
20	- `new WebSocket(url, protocols)`: no headers parameter; handshake headers are fixed, `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` comes from `protocols`. So the bearer header cannot be set from a page.
21	- If `protocols` is non-empty and the 101 does not carry a `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` acknowledging one, the connection fails. A server using the subprotocol route must echo exactly one of the offered values. (Answers the [run] question for browsers; the `tungstenite` side stays a test detail.)
22	- A failed handshake fires `error` then `close` with code 1006; the spec forbids exposing failure detail, so script cannot read a 401. The page must therefore check authority with a REST call (e.g. `GET /api/v1/info` or `/projects` with credentials) before and after a socket failure, and say "revoked"/"identity changed" from that, not from the socket.
23	- The handshake uses credentials mode `include`, so cookies for the origin are sent on it (same source). A fragment in the WebSocket URL throws. Queries: "WebSocket constructor protocols argument no custom headers; onerror no status code…".
24	
25	**Cookies**
26	- `HttpOnly` cookies are not readable via `document.cookie`; `Secure` cookies are sent only over https and insecure origins cannot set them (MDN: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Cookies). Any script on the origin can read `localStorage`; that is the Web Storage definition and the issue's statement stands.
27	- `SameSite=Strict` sends the cookie only for requests originating from the cookie's own site; `Lax` is the one that adds cross-site top-level navigation (MDN, same page; OWASP https://owasp.org/www-community/SameSite says a Strict cookie is withheld on a followed cross-site link). Consequence: the first load from a camera app is cross-site and carries no Strict cookie, which is fine for the pairing load (it has none yet) but means a bookmark or link tap shows the page before its cookie is sent; the page must make a same-origin `fetch` to learn state, which does carry it. Queries: "SameSite=Strict cookie withheld top-level navigation cross-site link…".
28	
29	**Certificate trust**
30	- Chrome ≥ 58 matches names only against the SAN and ignores the CN; a certificate without a matching SAN gives `NET::ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALID` (https://textslashplain.com/2017/03/10/chrome-deprecates-subject-cn-matching/, Chromium bug 700595 named there; Squid list https://ml-archives.squid-cache.org/squid-users/2017-May/015309.html agrees). Safari does not accept CN-only either (secondary: https://dev.to/dimastopel/why-subject-alternative-names-sans-matter-for-modern-browsers-30p0). Queries: "Chrome Safari self-signed certificate IP address no subject alternative name ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALID proceed unsafe"; "Chrome 58 certificate without subjectAltName…". No spike was run: every question the plan turns on is either settled by a source, answerable from the tree, or needs a device (owner). `git status` is clean.

**Tree (investigation's [tree] questions)**
- `RemoteReply { .. }` is built by struct literal at ~20 sites in `src/app.rs` (1664, 1679, 2365–2376, 2754, 3570, 3723, 3736, 3767 and others) plus `connection` in `src/adapters/remote.rs`; `RemoteRequest { .. }` literal only at its definition (`remote.rs:360`), none in `tests/`. A new header or cookie field on `RemoteReply` is a many-site change unless it goes through `envelope`/`refuse` (3730, 3754) or has a constructor default. Evidence: `grep -rn "RemoteReply {\|RemoteRequest {" src tests`.
- The QR payload is built inline inside `pairing(cx: &mut DrawCtx, ..)` at `src/ui/remote.rs:160–166`; it needs `cx.core.identity()`, `window` and `local_address()`. A URL form can be tested without egui only if the plan extracts a pure `fn(identity, window, address) -> String`.
- `SessionRecord` (`src/core/model.rs:1053`) is serialized; `SCHEMA_VERSION` is 16 (`model.rs:12`); the header says changes need a bump and a `migrate` step. A stored excerpt on the record is therefore a schema change; a per-list read of the last response is not a record change.
- Every request, including a page load, goes to the frame through the channel (`remote.rs:810–826`), and a connection stays in the 4-connection unauthenticated pool until its first authenticated reply (`remote.rs:701–706`, `835–849`). A static route answered through the frame inherits the pool; one answered on the connection thread would skip the frame and the `DRAIN_PER_PASS` bound. Rate windows key on exact `/api/v1/pair` and `/api/v1/info` only (`remote.rs:631–638`), so `/` and static paths are in no window unless the plan adds one. Tests that touch this: `pair_is_rate_limited_per_listener` and `a_wrong_pin_fails…` (`tests/remote.rs:1395–1411`) count requests to those two paths only, so a page route does not disturb them; `stalled_strangers_fill_their_own_pool…` (`tests/remote.rs:3226`) counts pool occupancy and is the one a page route must be run against.
- Revoked, unknown-token and rotated-key all answer the same 401 `unauthorized` (`app.rs:3142–3149`). Saying "revoked" plainly needs either a new error code (additive) or the page inferring it from `/info`: same `spki_sha256` and `server_id` as stored plus a 401 means revoked-or-unknown; a different key means identity changed.
- The certificate has no SAN, CN `Switchboard <server id>`, validity 1975–4096 (`remote.rs:101–106`; rcgen 0.14.10 defaults). The pin is of the key, so a certificate remade over the same key keeps every pin.

**Fragment and query**
- A URL fragment is not part of the request target and is not sent to the server; the `http`/`https` grammars exclude it. RFC 9110 §4.2.5: the fragment "does not appear in the ABNF definitions for the 'http' and 'https' URI schemes" (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#section-4.2.5); the HTTP messaging thread: "fragments are not part of the request-target and so are never transmitted" (https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2010AprJun/0070.html; Fielding: https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/uri/2004Feb/0125.html). Consequence: the query form `/?code=…` puts the code in the first `GET` request line to whoever answers TLS, before any script runs and before the key can be compared; `#code=…&key=…` keeps it out of the request, logs, and `Referer`. The query is in the request line by construction (request-target = path + query). Queries: "URL fragment identifier not sent to server in HTTP request RFC 3986 section 3.5".
- Caveat on the fragment: `history.replaceState` removal of the fragment is a script action after load; the plan builds to it either way.

**WebSocket in browsers (WHATWG WebSockets Standard, https://websockets.spec.whatwg.org/)**
- `new WebSocket(url, protocols)`: no headers parameter; handshake headers are fixed, `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` comes from `protocols`. So the bearer header cannot be set from a page.
- If `protocols` is non-empty and the 101 does not carry a `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` acknowledging one, the connection fails. A server using the subprotocol route must echo exactly one of the offered values. (Answers the [run] question for browsers; the `tungstenite` side stays a test detail.)
- A failed handshake fires `error` then `close` with code 1006; the spec forbids exposing failure detail, so script cannot read a 401. The page must therefore check authority with a REST call (e.g. `GET /api/v1/info` or `/projects` with credentials) before and after a socket failure, and say "revoked"/"identity changed" from that, not from the socket.
- The handshake uses credentials mode `include`, so cookies for the origin are sent on it (same source). A fragment in the WebSocket URL throws. Queries: "WebSocket constructor protocols argument no custom headers; onerror no status code…".

**Cookies**
- `HttpOnly` cookies are not readable via `document.cookie`; `Secure` cookies are sent only over https and insecure origins cannot set them (MDN: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Cookies). Any script on the origin can read `localStorage`; that is the Web Storage definition and the issue's statement stands.
- `SameSite=Strict` sends the cookie only for requests originating from the cookie's own site; `Lax` is the one that adds cross-site top-level navigation (MDN, same page; OWASP https://owasp.org/www-community/SameSite says a Strict cookie is withheld on a followed cross-site link). Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork runs in the background and keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate. Subagents run in the background; you'll be notified when one completes. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
