1	# Issue #230 — investigation notes
2	
3	Worktree: `/Users/sbgragent/.dispatch/worktrees/d12e42c9` (branch `dispatch/230-a-web-control-surface-the-remote-port-se`, HEAD `7fe8949`). Nothing was built, run or changed. Line numbers are from this tree.
4	
5	Read: `CLAUDE.md` (in the prompt), `docs/remote-client.md` (all of it), `docs/lessons.md`, `docs/design.md` (trust boundary 219–266, remote status 3107–3583, open questions 3672), `src/adapters/remote.rs` (outline; 355–660; 655–960), `src/app.rs` (3010–3170, 3568–3760, the drain at ~1572–1600, the subscribe path 2723–2760, the revoke hook 486–500), `src/core/remote.rs` (all), `src/ui/remote.rs` (all), `control/src/lib.rs` (the wire views), `src/core/events.rs` (124–140), `src/ui/cards.rs` (170–185, 558–575), `tests/remote.rs` (helpers 245–425, fixtures 1579–1840), the Swift invite code (`client/Sources/SwitchboardProtocol/Info.swift`, `client/Sources/switchboard-remote/main.swift`, `client/Tests/SwitchboardProtocolTests/FixturesTests.swift`, `client/Sources/SwitchboardClientCore/ConnectionManager.swift` 474–487, `client/Sources/SwitchboardUI/BrowserView.swift` 88–110, 849, 883).
6	
7	## What the issue touches, by file
8	
9	| Area | Where |
10	|---|---|
11	| Listener, pools, rate windows, request parse, response writer, WebSocket upgrade | `src/adapters/remote.rs`: `RemoteRequest` 360–372; `RemoteReply` 388–393; `read_request` 444–514; `respond_upgrade` 519–526; `respond` 530–552 (hard-codes `Content-Type: application/json` and `Connection: keep-alive`); `error_body` 556; pool sizes 567–568; deadlines 570–577; `DRAIN_PER_PASS` 580; `INBOX` 581; rate limits 583–587; `Limits::limited` 631–638 (only `/pair` and `/info`); `connection` 770–867; accept-time pool check 694–722; the subscriber loop 878–923 |
12	| Identity, certificate, pin, token and code makers | `src/adapters/remote.rs`: `make_identity` 95–128 (certificate params at 101–106); `tls_config` 144–158; `pinned_client` and the pin verifier 168–245; `pairing_code` 325; `bearer_token` 337; `token_sha256` 345; `local_address` 962–975 |
13	| Path split, allowlist, auth, pairing, info, revoke, events | `src/app.rs`: `serve_pending` 1572 (drains remote requests at ~1587); `serve_remote` 3017–3123 (non-`/api/v1/` path refused at 3023–3025; `/info` and `/pair` before auth at 3027–3031); `authenticate` 3127–3152; `remote_command` 3159 (body `op`, `text`; scope check 3166); `remote_info` 3568–3599; `remote_pair` 3606–3673; `remote_reply` 3695; `envelope` 3730; `refuse` 3754 (logs method, path, code); `event_json` 2646–2659; `remote_subscribe` 2723–2760; the bind by `listen.lan` 2962–2969; the revoke hook that drops subscribers 486–500 |
14	| Pairing state and devices | `src/core/remote.rs`: pairing actions 46–64; `Paired` 65–71 (closes the window); `DeviceSeen` 72–85 (saves last-seen at most every 300 s, constant at 18); `RevokeDevice` 86–92; `SetDeviceScope` 93–100; `device_by_token` 145–147; `pairing_at` 152–154; `new_device` 166–175 (name trimmed to 64 characters; scope from the window). `PAIRING_WINDOW` is `src/core/action.rs:972`. Device record type: `src/ports/remote.rs:96` |
15	| Pairing window, QR, dialog | `src/ui/remote.rs`: the trust sentence in the dialog 70–76; the pairing window 141–227; the QR payload is built inline at 160–166 (`server_id`, `spki_sha256`, `code`, `addresses`); `addresses` comes from `local_address()` at 157–164 whatever the listen setting; "Copy invite" copies the JSON at 199–206; the devices list with scope and Revoke 230–276; `qr_texture` 280–299 |
16	| Wire views for the page | `control/src/lib.rs` `SessionView` 637–689 (`card`, `waiting`, `waiting_reason`, `trust_question`, `resume_id`, `op`, `transcript`, `last_activity_ms`); `ProjectView` 691 on |
17	| Routes the page would call | `GET /api/v1/info`, `POST /api/v1/pair`, `GET /api/v1/projects`, `/projects/{id}/sessions`, `/waiting`, `/sessions/{id}`, `/sessions/{id}/last-response` (routed at `app.rs:1967` and `3101`), `/sessions/{id}/screen`, `POST /sessions/{id}/send`, `GET /api/v1/events` (upgrade) |
18	| Native pairing text path | `client/Sources/SwitchboardProtocol/Info.swift`: `ServerInfo` 4–38; `PairRequest` 41–63; `PairReply` 65–79; `PairingInvite` 94–116, parsed as JSON only (`Wire.decode`, 113–116). `client/Sources/switchboard-remote/main.swift`: usage 9–16; `pair` with one argument parses JSON at 111; with three arguments builds the invite at 118; device name `"<host> (cli)"` at 33. `BrowserView.swift` 103–107 (the launch-time `SWITCHBOARD_INVITE` path) and 849, 883 (the headset's paste field). `ConnectionManager.swift` 474–487 |
19	| Trust text and status | `docs/design.md` "Trust boundary" 219–266 (the redacted-text sentence at 249–252); remote status 3107–3583 |
20	| Tests | `tests/remote.rs`: `http` 245–297 (hand-rolled TLS client, reads `Content-Length` bodies only); `call` 299–325 (asserts the body is JSON); `get` 327; `pair` helper 406–424; `pool` and rate tests 1395–1421 (`a_wrong_pin…`, `pair_is_rate_limited_per_listener`); `stalled_strangers_fill_their_own_pool…` 3226; `write_fixtures` 1585; the fixture gate 1829–1833 (writes only when `SWITCHBOARD_WRITE_FIXTURES` is set). `tests/ui.rs` 7420–7503 drives the dialog. `client/Tests/SwitchboardProtocolTests/FixturesTests.swift` 157–165 inlines the invite JSON |
21	
22	Not present in the tree: a `web/` directory, any `include_str!` in `src/` (no precedent for embedded assets), any cookie or `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` handling, any `Origin` or `Host` check, any `User-Agent` capture, and any Rust test of the QR payload.
23	
24	## Record and rehydration first, then the page
25	
26	**A paired browser (device record).** On disk: `devices.json` holds a `PairedDevice` made in `new_device` (`core/remote.rs:166–175`): `id`, `name` (the body's `device_name`, trimmed, at most 64 characters), `scope` (from the pairing window), `token_sha256`, `created`, `last_seen`. The token itself is never stored on the host. Rehydration: `IdentityLoaded` loads the devices (`core/remote.rs:23–31`), and each request finds its device by hash (`app.rs:3137–3140`). The reply to `/pair` carries `token`, `scope`, `server_id`, `device_id` in the JSON body (`app.rs:3660–3672`). Today the browser would keep that token in its own storage, which the host knows nothing about. Pane: the paired-devices row (`ui/remote.rs:241–275`) shows name, scope, paired and seen times, and Revoke. Nothing in the tree gives a device its own scope or name back (no `/me` route; `scope` in `/info` is the listing parameter, not a device property).
27	
28	**The pairing window.** In memory only, never saved (`core/remote.rs:46–54`, `Effect` absent). A restart closes it. Its code is compared at `app.rs:3646`; a wrong key counts too, at `3636–3645`, so a page that sends the wrong `key` spends one of three attempts. The host ignores any `server_id` in the request: `remote_pair` reads only `spki_sha256`, `code` and `device_name` (`app.rs:3626–3655`). The QR and the text are built from `identity` and `window` at render time (`ui/remote.rs:160–166`), not stored.
29	
30	**The page's own state.** On disk: nothing on the host. In the browser: whatever the page keeps. The tree has no browser storage, so the server id, pinned key, scope and host name the page needs on a later visit have no source except the page's own storage, or a new endpoint.
31	
32	**The session list.** Rehydrated per request from the core's views (`app.rs:3044–3059`, `3119–3121` hides Dispatch worker records unless `scope=all`). Each row would show `name`, `kind`, `card` (the card's word), `waiting` and `waiting_reason`. There is no excerpt field on `SessionView` (`control/src/lib.rs:637–689`). The Mac card computes its excerpt in the UI: for an agent, the first line of the last answer from the transcript, or the last activity line, or the prompt (`ui/cards.rs:176–180`, `558–575`); for others, the pane caption or the host title (`ui/cards.rs:180–185`). Pane: the list grouped by project, waiting ones first. The waiting mark and the card word are on the wire. The one-line excerpt is not.
33	
34	**The last response and the screen.** On disk: the agent's transcript JSONL (its path is `SessionView.transcript`, `control/src/lib.rs:687`), read and parsed on the content path (`app.rs:1967`, `3101`). The pane's text is not on disk; it is a tmux snapshot (`screen` route, `app.rs:3101`). Pane: the last answer, or the screen for a session without a conversation. A change arrives as `changed {conversation|screen, id}` from the poll; the page refetches on it. Event payloads carry no body: `event_json` (`app.rs:2646–2659`) sends only type, resource, revision and time.
35	
36	**A reply.** Rehydration on the host: the `send` body is `{op, text}` (`app.rs:3180–3205`, `text` trimmed, at most 16 KiB, checked at 3193). The op goes to `operations.log` before the keys are sent (design.md A3 status, "The control port's `serve` logs a non-replayable command's request line before it runs"). A repeat of the op is answered from the log; an op with a request line and no reply is `interrupted` and never run again. Pane: the page shows the send accepted; progress is the session's state moving (`PromptSubmitted`, working, `Stop`, spec §4.5 line 279). The page can't know the reply went through until a `changed` frame arrives. A session at Claude's folder-trust question takes the text nowhere until `trust` answers it (`trust_question`, `control/src/lib.rs:662`).
37	
38	**Revocation and identity change.** Revoke removes the `PairedDevice` (`core/remote.rs:86–92`) and drops the device's subscribers, which closes their sockets (`app.rs:486–500`, `adapters/remote.rs:890–902`). The next request from that token gets 401 with code `unauthorized` and the message "the token is not known; pair again" (`app.rs:3142–3149`). That is the same code and message an unknown token gets, and a rotated key gets it too. So the tree cannot tell the page "revoked" from "never paired" or "key rotated" today. A changed key shows on `/info` as a different `spki_sha256` (`app.rs:3581`, `identity.spki_sha256`), which the page can compare with the one it stored. A WebSocket handshake refused with 401 is a plain non-101 response (`app.rs:3036–3038`, `adapters/remote.rs:864`).
39	
40	**The first load from a QR.** Today `GET /?code=…` gets `serve_remote`'s JSON 404 (`app.rs:3023–3025`), not a page. Every request reaches the frame through the bounded channel (`adapters/remote.rs:810–825`); the frame drains 8 per pass (`DRAIN_PER_PASS`, `remote.rs:580`, `app.rs:~1587`). The unauthenticated pool is 4 connections, counted at accept (`remote.rs:701–706`), and a connection stays in it until its first authenticated reply (`remote.rs:835–849`). A keep-alive connection after its first request has a 30 s idle timeout (`remote.rs:573`, `783–787`); before the first request the read timeout is the 5 s handshake timeout (`remote.rs:771`). The rate windows apply only to `/api/v1/pair` (6 a minute) and `/api/v1/info` (60 a minute), keyed by exact path (`remote.rs:583–587`, `631–638`); a page path is in neither.
41	
42	**The certificate a browser would see.** The certificate has no subject alternative names; it is made with an empty name list and a common name `Switchboard <server id>` (`remote.rs:101–106`). Its validity is rcgen 0.14.10's default, 1975-01-01 to 4096-01-01 (`~/.cargo/registry/src/*/rcgen-0.14.10/src/certificate.rs:83–85`). The LAN address the page would be opened at is the outbound-route address (`remote.rs:962–975`), so no fixed IP can be put in the certificate. The SPKI pin is unaffected (the pin is of the key, `remote.rs:168–245`, and `remote-client.md` §5).
43	
44	**The listen address.** The listener binds the LAN interface only when `listen.lan` is set (`app.rs:2962–2969`), but the QR's address comes from `local_address()` regardless (`ui/remote.rs:157–164`). With the listen off, the QR names an address the port does not answer on. This is in the tree today, not new.
45	
46	## Decision facts from the tree
47	
48	1. **Browser trust.** Facts: no SAN, CN only, 1975–4096 validity (above); the code travels in the URL's query and so in the first `GET` (`src/ui/remote.rs:160–166` puts `code` in the payload the issue would turn into a query); `refuse` logs method, path and code name, not the query (`app.rs:3754–3772`), so the host itself does not log the code. `remote-client.md` §5 line 306 ("Require pairing before anything but `/info` and `/pair`") and line 319 (no non-loopback bind without pairing) are the rules the page would amend. A page served before pairing is a new allowlist entry; `serve_remote` refuses every non-`/api/v1/` path today.
49	2. **Token transport.** `read_request` takes only `Authorization: Bearer` (`remote.rs:487–490`); no cookie, no `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` (`remote.rs:491–494` takes `Upgrade` and `Sec-WebSocket-Key` only). `respond_upgrade` writes `Upgrade`, `Connection` and `Sec-WebSocket-Accept` and no protocol (`remote.rs:519–526`). `RemoteReply` has no header field (`remote.rs:388–393`); `respond` writes one fixed header set (`remote.rs:530–552`). The `/pair` reply is `envelope(200, &reply, false)` (`app.rs:3672`), so its token is in JSON and the connection is not marked authenticated. Nothing checks `Origin` or `Host` (grep of `src/adapters/remote.rs` and `src/app.rs`). `remote-client.md` §5 line 312: the token "is sent only as a bearer header over the pinned connection, never in a URL", and §7 line 352 says the client keeps its token in the Keychain, which a browser has no equivalent of.
50	3. **One QR or two.** Every consumer of the invite parses JSON: the CLI (`main.swift` 111), `PairingInvite.parse` (`Info.swift` 113–116), the headset paste (`BrowserView.swift` 883), the launch variable (`BrowserView.swift` 103–107). The Rust side builds the payload but never parses it. The Swift invite test uses an inline JSON string (`FixturesTests.swift` 157–165), not a file from `client/Fixtures/`.
51	4. **Static paths.** No route; every path other than `/api/v1/` is refused (`app.rs:3023–3025`). `respond` is JSON-only (`remote.rs:530–552`). Static bytes don't need the frame, but `connection()` sends every request to the frame (`remote.rs:810–826`), so a static route on the connection thread would be a second path; nothing in the tree has one.

1	# Facts for issue #230 (web control surface)
2	
3	No spike was run: every question the plan turns on is either settled by a source, answerable from the tree, or needs a device (owner). `git status` is clean.
4	
5	## Settled
6	
7	**Tree (investigation's [tree] questions)**
8	- `RemoteReply { .. }` is built by struct literal at ~20 sites in `src/app.rs` (1664, 1679, 2365–2376, 2754, 3570, 3723, 3736, 3767 and others) plus `connection` in `src/adapters/remote.rs`; `RemoteRequest { .. }` literal only at its definition (`remote.rs:360`), none in `tests/`. A new header or cookie field on `RemoteReply` is a many-site change unless it goes through `envelope`/`refuse` (3730, 3754) or has a constructor default. Evidence: `grep -rn "RemoteReply {\|RemoteRequest {" src tests`.
9	- The QR payload is built inline inside `pairing(cx: &mut DrawCtx, ..)` at `src/ui/remote.rs:160–166`; it needs `cx.core.identity()`, `window` and `local_address()`. A URL form can be tested without egui only if the plan extracts a pure `fn(identity, window, address) -> String`.
10	- `SessionRecord` (`src/core/model.rs:1053`) is serialized; `SCHEMA_VERSION` is 16 (`model.rs:12`); the header says changes need a bump and a `migrate` step. A stored excerpt on the record is therefore a schema change; a per-list read of the last response is not a record change.
11	- Every request, including a page load, goes to the frame through the channel (`remote.rs:810–826`), and a connection stays in the 4-connection unauthenticated pool until its first authenticated reply (`remote.rs:701–706`, `835–849`). A static route answered through the frame inherits the pool; one answered on the connection thread would skip the frame and the `DRAIN_PER_PASS` bound. Rate windows key on exact `/api/v1/pair` and `/api/v1/info` only (`remote.rs:631–638`), so `/` and static paths are in no window unless the plan adds one. Tests that touch this: `pair_is_rate_limited_per_listener` and `a_wrong_pin_fails…` (`tests/remote.rs:1395–1411`) count requests to those two paths only, so a page route does not disturb them; `stalled_strangers_fill_their_own_pool…` (`tests/remote.rs:3226`) counts pool occupancy and is the one a page route must be run against.
12	- Revoked, unknown-token and rotated-key all answer the same 401 `unauthorized` (`app.rs:3142–3149`). Saying "revoked" plainly needs either a new error code (additive) or the page inferring it from `/info`: same `spki_sha256` and `server_id` as stored plus a 401 means revoked-or-unknown; a different key means identity changed.
13	- The certificate has no SAN, CN `Switchboard <server id>`, validity 1975–4096 (`remote.rs:101–106`; rcgen 0.14.10 defaults). The pin is of the key, so a certificate remade over the same key keeps every pin.
14	
15	**Fragment and query**
16	- A URL fragment is not part of the request target and is not sent to the server; the `http`/`https` grammars exclude it. RFC 9110 §4.2.5: the fragment "does not appear in the ABNF definitions for the 'http' and 'https' URI schemes" (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#section-4.2.5); the HTTP messaging thread: "fragments are not part of the request-target and so are never transmitted" (https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2010AprJun/0070.html; Fielding: https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/uri/2004Feb/0125.html). Consequence: the query form `/?code=…` puts the code in the first `GET` request line to whoever answers TLS, before any script runs and before the key can be compared; `#code=…&key=…` keeps it out of the request, logs, and `Referer`. The query is in the request line by construction (request-target = path + query). Queries: "URL fragment identifier not sent to server in HTTP request RFC 3986 section 3.5".
17	- Caveat on the fragment: `history.replaceState` removal of the fragment is a script action after load; the plan builds to it either way.
18	
19	**WebSocket in browsers (WHATWG WebSockets Standard, https://websockets.spec.whatwg.org/)**
20	- `new WebSocket(url, protocols)`: no headers parameter; handshake headers are fixed, `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` comes from `protocols`. So the bearer header cannot be set from a page.
21	- If `protocols` is non-empty and the 101 does not carry a `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` acknowledging one, the connection fails. A server using the subprotocol route must echo exactly one of the offered values. (Answers the [run] question for browsers; the `tungstenite` side stays a test detail.)
22	- A failed handshake fires `error` then `close` with code 1006; the spec forbids exposing failure detail, so script cannot read a 401. The page must therefore check authority with a REST call (e.g. `GET /api/v1/info` or `/projects` with credentials) before and after a socket failure, and say "revoked"/"identity changed" from that, not from the socket.
23	- The handshake uses credentials mode `include`, so cookies for the origin are sent on it (same source). A fragment in the WebSocket URL throws. Queries: "WebSocket constructor protocols argument no custom headers; onerror no status code…".
24	
25	**Cookies**
26	- `HttpOnly` cookies are not readable via `document.cookie`; `Secure` cookies are sent only over https and insecure origins cannot set them (MDN: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Cookies). Any script on the origin can read `localStorage`; that is the Web Storage definition and the issue's statement stands.
27	- `SameSite=Strict` sends the cookie only for requests originating from the cookie's own site; `Lax` is the one that adds cross-site top-level navigation (MDN, same page; OWASP https://owasp.org/www-community/SameSite says a Strict cookie is withheld on a followed cross-site link). Consequence: the first load from a camera app is cross-site and carries no Strict cookie, which is fine for the pairing load (it has none yet) but means a bookmark or link tap shows the page before its cookie is sent; the page must make a same-origin `fetch` to learn state, which does carry it. Queries: "SameSite=Strict cookie withheld top-level navigation cross-site link…".
28	
29	**Certificate trust**
30	- Chrome ≥ 58 matches names only against the SAN and ignores the CN; a certificate without a matching SAN gives `NET::ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALID` (https://textslashplain.com/2017/03/10/chrome-deprecates-subject-cn-matching/, Chromium bug 700595 named there; Squid list https://ml-archives.squid-cache.org/squid-users/2017-May/015309.html agrees). Safari does not accept CN-only either (secondary: https://dev.to/dimastopel/why-subject-alternative-names-sans-matter-for-modern-browsers-30p0). Queries: "Chrome Safari self-signed certificate IP address no subject alternative name ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALID proceed unsafe"; "Chrome 58 certificate without subjectAltName…". Plan must build to: the certificate gains an IP SAN for the address in the URL regardless of whether click-through is offered (see Unresolved 1 for what that costs).
31	- Apple's 398-day limit applies only to certificates from preinstalled roots; user-added roots are exempt (https://support.apple.com/en-qa/102028, page dated 2023-08-21). The 1975–4096 validity therefore does not by itself break a download-and-trust path. Whether a *self-signed leaf with a user exception* is held to it is not stated there (Unresolved 2).
32	- **Safari (iOS, iPadOS, Apple-silicon macOS) does not support `wss://` to a self-signed or otherwise invalid certificate, even when manually trusted**; the workaround Cockpit documents is a valid certificate, or the "NSURLSession WebSocket" experimental flag in Settings > Safari > Advanced > Experimental Features (https://cockpit-project.org/running/safari, footer 2026; history: WebKit list thread https://lists.webkit.org/pipermail/webkit-dev/2011-June/017335.html "Allow wss:// if user has accepted https:// warning?", and WebKit bug 158345 (open) records the switch to NSURLSession WebSockets as experimental). No source contradicts. Queries: "Safari \"Show Details\" \"visit this website\" certificate exception IP address WebSocket wss self-signed iOS". Consequence the plan must carry: on Safari the events socket may never connect over a click-through certificate. The page needs a polling path on the same REST routes (re-read `/waiting` and the open session on an interval, applying replies by revision per §4.4), used when the socket fails; the "moves to the top without a reload" acceptance step must be met by polling on iOS Safari unless the owner's trust step installs the certificate (Unresolved 2).
33	
34	## Unresolved
35	
36	1. **Does Chrome/Safari offer click-through for a SAN-less certificate on an IP-literal address, and does the exception persist and cover the same origin?** Tried: the queries above plus "Chromium net error ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALID overridable…"; results were forum posts and said only that HSTS or policy can remove the proceed link, nothing on persistence or scope. Not settled by two qualifying sources. Build to: *favourable* → click-through is the trust step as the issue's option one, said in the paired-devices dialog. *Unfavourable or unknown* → the plan still adds the IP SAN to the certificate (remade over the same key, so pins hold) and ships the certificate download (option two) as the documented path; it must not depend on the click-through working.
37	2. **Does a downloaded certificate/profile become usable on iOS only after Certificate Trust Settings → full trust, and does it then fix `wss://`?** Tried: "Safari iOS certificate validity period 398 days user exception self-signed trust" (found only the Apple scope note above). Build to: *favourable* → the download path gives the iOS user a working socket; *unfavourable* → polling fallback (above) is the iOS path and the socket is an enhancement. The plan builds the polling path either way.
38	3. **Do Safari and Chrome store and send a `Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict` host-only cookie set from a user-accepted certificate on an IP-literal host?** Tried: MDN Cookies page (silent on IP hosts and on exceptions), "SameSite=Strict cookie withheld…" (silent). Build to: *favourable* → cookie transport (decision 2). *Unfavourable* → fall back to the token held by the page (storage) with the `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` echo for the socket, which the WHATWG source above shows works mechanically; the host keeps accepting the bearer header. Because Safari may not give the socket at all (Settled), the REST path needs the same credential: the plan should make the credential accepted on REST from a cookie *or* header so the polling fallback works under either outcome.
39	4. **Does `history.replaceState` leave the full URL in an earlier history entry or tab list in Safari?** Tried: not searched past the first round of queries; no source. Build to: if the fragment form is used, the code never reaches the server; the page still calls `replaceState` first and clears the fragment, and the dialog says the code is single-use and the window closes on pairing (`core/remote.rs:65`), which makes a leaked URL inert after pairing either way.
40	5. **Does the iOS camera pass the `https://` URL unchanged, and does iOS Safari prompt for Local Network permission on a LAN IP?** Tried: not searched; device behaviour. See owner.
41	6. **How many connections a browser opens per page load, idle keep-alive hold time, and unprompted `/favicon.ico`.** Not searched. Build to: the page route and `/favicon.ico` must answer (or 404 cheaply) through the same unauthenticated pool, and closing a connection after a static reply (`Connection: close`) avoids holding one of the four slots for 30 s (`remote.rs:573`); the plan decides on that basis. A run against the harness with five parallel connections settles the pool count if the plan wants a number.
42	
43	## For the owner
44	
45	- On the phone, scan the QR (or open the URL), proceed past the certificate warning: does the page load? Branch: yes → click-through is the documented trust step; no → certificate download path (Unresolved 1/2). The plan builds the download path unless this is confirmed.
46	- On iOS Safari after proceeding: does `changed` arrive without a reload (socket connected), or only after polling? Branch: connects → socket primary; does not → polling is primary on iOS (built either way).
47	- Does the phone reach the Mac (listen setting on, no access-point isolation), and does Safari show the Local Network prompt? Branch: reachable → acceptance steps 1–4; not → nothing the plan can change; the dialog states the listen requirement. Note the QR address is `local_address()` even when `listen.lan` is off (`ui/remote.rs:157–164`), so the plan should omit or flag the address when the listener is loopback.
48	- After revoking the phone, does the page show "revoked" on its next request? Branch: with a distinct code or the `/info` comparison, yes in both cases the plan builds the page to say it.

| GET | `/api/v1/dispatch/tickets` | new: the core's `TicketListing` (§4.7) | read |
| GET | `/api/v1/dispatch/tickets/{id}` | new: `TicketDetail` | read |
| POST | `/api/v1/dispatch/tickets/{id}/decide` | new: the Mac's `DispatchDecide` | control |
| POST | `/api/v1/dispatch/tickets/{id}/resume` | new: the Mac's `DispatchResume` | control |
| POST | `/api/v1/dispatch/tickets/{id}/close` | new: the Mac's `DispatchClose` | control |
| GET | `/api/v1/dispatch/tickets/{id}/files/{key}` | new: the Mac's `DispatchReadArtifact`, or the disk for an image | read |
| GET | `/api/v1/dispatch/tickets/{id}/events` | new: the Mac's `DispatchReadEvents` | read |
| GET | `/api/v1/events` | WebSocket upgrade | read |

Everything else on the wire is **refused before translation**, by an allowlist, not a denylist: `env.resolve` returns secret values; the `env.*` writes, `definition.install`, `project.add`, `project.root`, `set.sync`, `workflow.*`, `dispatch.runner`, `session.kill` and `session.remove` change what runs on the host or what it keeps. v1 remote is the table above and nothing more.

**Redaction, one policy for every text that leaves the port, applied before any cut.** `session.screen` today masks the values of the project's secret variables and of the session's granted environment sets, and it reads slack lines above the window first so a value wrapped across the window's first line is still found whole. The port generalizes both halves of that: one `redact` function in `app.rs`, and the rule that **masking runs over complete source text, and every cut comes after**, since a value split by a cut no longer matches. Per kind:
  - **conversation**: the parser caps tool detail at `DETAIL_CAP` while parsing, so masking a parsed turn would miss a value crossing that cap. The transcript reader gains an additive `read_masked(handle, &dyn Fn(&str) -> String)` that applies the mask to every string field before `cap`; the port's conversation cache (§4.4) is populated through it, keyed by the secret set's fingerprint as well, and is separate from the UI's unmasked cache. The 256 KiB turn cut then runs on masked text.
  - **run output**: `scrollback::tail_text` cuts bytes before stripping escapes and choosing lines. It gains an overlap: the read starts `longest secret length` bytes before the tail window, the mask runs over the whole buffer, and the line selection then discards the overlap; a value straddling the window's first byte is therefore masked whole. A secret value containing a newline is masked only within a line, which the dialog's sentence on redaction covers.
  - **screen**: the existing slack-lines read, unchanged.
  - **file content**: the file is read whole under its limit, masked, then sent.
  - **last response** and the card excerpt: masked from the turn's full text, then cut.
  The secret set for a session is the project's secret variables plus its granted sets; for a file it is the owning project's. The set is resolved **before any cached content is returned**, on every read, and its **policy fingerprint** (a hash over the sorted names and values, held in memory only, never logged or stored) is part of every masked cache's version (§4.4): a new grant, a changed value or a removed set makes previously masked bytes stale even when their source did not move. ## 5. Security and pairing

A local network is not a trust boundary: these APIs can instruct coding agents and expose private transcripts. The repo's rules apply unchanged: secret values never reach a record, a log line, a command line, or any reply but `env.resolve` (which is not on this port) and, as redacted text, the read models of §4.3; the Keychain holds key material.

- Require pairing **before** anything but `/info` and `/pair`.
- **Host identity**: a self-signed certificate made once with `rcgen` on first listen. The certificate is in `identity.json` (§3.1); its private key is a Keychain item through the existing adapter (`adapters/keychain.rs`, service `com.sadburger.switchboard`) under the account `remote-key:<server_id>`, so two data directories under one macOS account never overwrite each other's keys. The bundle must be signed with the stable identity (`scripts/bundle.sh`) or the Keychain ACL is lost on every rebuild.
- **What the client pins** is the SPKI SHA-256 of the host's public key, not the certificate's bytes, so a certificate reissued from the same key (a new expiry) still verifies. Rotating the key is making a new identity: every pairing is invalid and the dialog says so.
- **Pairing verifies the key before the code is sent.** The code alone would let an intermediary terminate the first connection, forward the code to the real host, and take the token. So the pairing window shows a **QR code** carrying `{server_id, spki_sha256, code, addresses}`, and under it the same in text: a short form of the key hash and the code. The client scans or types both; it connects, compares the hash of the key it is actually talking to with the one it was given, and only when they match sends `/pair {code, device_name, spki_sha256}`. A client without a camera (visionOS gives an app none) pairs from the host's Bonjour record instead: it resolves the record, reads `/info` under no trust, shows the key the host presented in the dialog's short form for the owner to compare by eye, and pins that key for the pairing, so the typed code reaches only the host whose key the owner checked; a substituted certificate shows its own key on the device, where the owner sees it differ. The host refuses a pairing whose `spki_sha256` is not its own, so a relayed request through a substituted certificate fails even if the code reached it. Before pairing, `/info` is served to any client and nothing in it is trusted; after pairing, every connection verifies the pin before the token is presented.
- The pairing window is opened from the settings menu as "Allow pairing for 5 minutes", the same shape as the environment setup window (`ENV_SETUP_WINDOW`, never saved). The dialog that opens it chooses the scope the pairing grants, `read` by default.
- **The code**: eight characters from the 32-character Crockford alphabet (no `I`, `L`, `O`, `U`), 40 bits, drawn from the OS random source (`getrandom`), made when the window opens and shown as the QR's `code` and in text. It is single-use: the first successful `/pair` consumes it and closes the window. **Failures count globally**: one counter in the app's state, bumped on the frame for every failed `/pair` from any connection, and the window closes at three. Concurrent attempts cannot each get three, because the frame answers them in arrival order against the one counter.
- **The token**: 32 bytes from the OS random source, base64url, 43 characters. It does not expire; the owner revokes. It is sent only as a bearer header over the pinned connection, never in a URL.
- `/pair` answers with the token and the granted scope. The host stores the device name, scope, created time, last-seen time and the token's SHA-256 in `<data dir>/devices.json` (atomic write, owner-readable); never the token. The client stores the token and the pinned key hash in its Keychain.
- **Scope changes** happen in the host's dialog: a device's scope can be raised to `control` or lowered to `read` there, taking effect on the device's next request. There is no scope request over the port.
- **Key rotation** (a missing key at listen, §3.1) **deletes every record in `devices.json`** when the new identity is made, so an old token stops working on the first request, and the dialog says the pairings are gone. A client seeing a new key for a known `server_id` shows "identity changed, pair again" and sends nothing, token included.
- Every later request carries the bearer token; the host answers with the device's scope. A Settings dialog (built the way the Environment dialog is) lists paired devices with scope, last seen, and Revoke, and states what redaction does and does not cover. Revocation removes the record, takes effect on the next request and closes the device's WebSocket.
- The client verifies the pin on every connection and on endpoint changes; a mismatch is shown as "identity changed, pair again" and never auto-merged.
- Validate input, cap request bodies at 64 KiB, cap `lines` on `screen` (the wire clamps to 200) and `run_output` (500), cap pages and bodies as §4.2 says, and keep tokens out of logs, URLs, Bonjour TXT records and crash reports. Refusals are logged by op and kind, never with content.
- Loopback-only without auth is acceptable **only inside the spike directory**. No milestone commit binds a non-loopback interface without pairing.

The repo's rules apply unchanged: secret values never reach a record, a log line, a command line, or any reply but `env.resolve` (which is not on this port) and, as redacted text, the read models of §4.3; the Keychain holds key material.

- Require pairing **before** anything but `/info` and `/pair`.
- **Host identity**: a self-signed certificate made once with `rcgen` on first listen. The certificate is in `identity.json` (§3.1); its private key is a Keychain item through the existing adapter (`adapters/keychain.rs`, service `com.sadburger.switchboard`) under the account `remote-key:<server_id>`, so two data directories under one macOS account never overwrite each other's keys. The bundle must be signed with the stable identity (`scripts/bundle.sh`) or the Keychain ACL is lost on every rebuild.
- **What the client pins** is the SPKI SHA-256 of the host's public key, not the certificate's bytes, so a certificate reissued from the same key (a new expiry) still verifies. Rotating the key is making a new identity: every pairing is invalid and the dialog says so.
- **Pairing verifies the key before the code is sent.** The code alone would let an intermediary terminate the first connection, forward the code to the real host, and take the token. So the pairing window shows a **QR code** carrying `{server_id, spki_sha256, code, addresses}`, and under it the same in text: a short form of the key hash and the code. The client scans or types both; it connects, compares the hash of the key it is actually talking to with the one it was given, and only when they match sends `/pair {code, device_name, spki_sha256}`. A client without a camera (visionOS gives an app none) pairs from the host's Bonjour record instead: it resolves the record, reads `/info` under no trust, shows the key the host presented in the dialog's short form for the owner to compare by eye, and pins that key for the pairing, so the typed code reaches only the host whose key the owner checked; a substituted certificate shows its own key on the device, where the owner sees it differ. The host refuses a pairing whose `spki_sha256` is not its own, so a relayed request through a substituted certificate fails even if the code reached it. Before pairing, `/info` is served to any client and nothing in it is trusted; after pairing, every connection verifies the pin before the token is presented.
- The pairing window is opened from the settings menu as "Allow pairing for 5 minutes", the same shape as the environment setup window (`ENV_SETUP_WINDOW`, never saved). The dialog that opens it chooses the scope the pairing grants, `read` by default.
- **The code**: eight characters from the 32-character Crockford alphabet (no `I`, `L`, `O`, `U`), 40 bits, drawn from the OS random source (`getrandom`), made when the window opens and shown as the QR's `code` and in text. It is single-use: the first successful `/pair` consumes it and closes the window. **Failures count globally**: one counter in the app's state, bumped on the frame for every failed `/pair` from any connection, and the window closes at three. Concurrent attempts cannot each get three, because the frame answers them in arrival order against the one counter.
- **The token**: 32 bytes from the OS random source, base64url, 43 characters. It does not expire; the owner revokes. It is sent only as a bearer header over the pinned connection, never in a URL.
- `/pair` answers with the token and the granted scope. The host stores the device name, scope, created time, last-seen time and the token's SHA-256 in `<data dir>/devices.json` (atomic write, owner-readable); never the token. The client stores the token and the pinned key hash in its Keychain.
- **Scope changes** happen in the host's dialog: a device's scope can be raised to `control` or lowered to `read` there, taking effect on the device's next request. There is no scope request over the port.
- **Key rotation** (a missing key at listen, §3.1) **deletes every record in `devices.json`** when the new identity is made, so an old token stops working on the first request, and the dialog says the pairings are gone. A client seeing a new key for a known `server_id` shows "identity changed, pair again" and sends nothing, token included.
- Every later request carries the bearer token; the host answers with the device's scope. A Settings dialog (built the way the Environment dialog is) lists paired devices with scope, last seen, and Revoke, and states what redaction does and does not cover. Revocation removes the record, takes effect on the next request and closes the device's WebSocket.
- The client verifies the pin on every connection and on endpoint changes; a mismatch is shown as "identity changed, pair again" and never auto-merged.
- Validate input, cap request bodies at 64 KiB, cap `lines` on `screen` (the wire clamps to 200) and `run_output` (500), cap pages and bodies as §4.2 says, and keep tokens out of logs, URLs, Bonjour TXT records and crash reports. Refusals are logged by op and kind, never with content.
- Loopback-only without auth is acceptable **only inside the spike directory**. No milestone commit binds a non-loopback interface without pairing.

# Plan: a web control surface on the remote port (#230)

The host serves a small page from the port it already has. A phone opens it from the pairing window's QR, pairs, lists the sessions with the waiting ones first, reads a session's last response or screen, and sends a reply. The page is three embedded files (`web/index.html`, `web/app.js`, `web/app.css`) with no build step and no dependency. It speaks the protocol the headset speaks.

Yardstick for the world outside this tree: `facts.md` for #230. Where a decision rests on a line under Settled, the line is cited. Where it rests on a line under Unresolved or For the owner, the decision says so, and the default is the design that works whichever way the answer goes. Line numbers are from this worktree at `7fe8949`.

## Where this departs from the issue

- **The code travels in the URL fragment, not the query.** The issue's `/?code=…&key=…&id=…` puts the code in the request line of the first `GET`, so a server the owner has not verified receives it before any script runs, and `read_request` hands the query to the frame (`src/adapters/remote.rs:495–503`). A fragment is not part of the request target and is never sent (Settled, "Fragment and query"; RFC 9110 §4.2.5). The URL is `https://<address>:<port>/#code=<code>&key=<spki_sha256>&id=<server_id>`. The page still calls `history.replaceState` before anything else; whether Safari keeps the full URL in an earlier history entry is Unresolved 4, so the code's single use does the rest: `Paired` closes the window (`src/core/remote.rs:65`), and a leaked URL is inert after the first pairing.
- **The key in the URL is not authentication in a browser.** The issue says the comparison lets a genuine page refuse to send the code to a host whose `/info` key differs. A browser cannot see which certificate it is talking to, so a relay that terminates TLS and forwards to the real host shows the page the real key and the comparison passes. The plan keeps the comparison (it catches a QR for another host, and a stale one) and says in the dialog that it is not a defence. A browser pairing is weaker than a native one, which pins the key out of band; the dialog says "pair a browser only on a network you trust".
- **The one-line excerpt is not on the wire, and the spec says it is.** `docs/remote-client.md:207` says the card's excerpt is `last_message` from the `Stop` hook "on the record". `src/core/events.rs:127–135` stores only `last_stop_at` and `pending_at_stop`; `SessionView` (`control/src/lib.rs:637–689`) has no excerpt; the Mac computes it in the UI from the transcript (`src/ui/cards.rs:176–185`, `558–575`). Storing it would change `SessionRecord` (`src/core/model.rs:1053`, `SCHEMA_VERSION` 16) and moving the function would be a change of its own. This cut: a row shows the name, kind, the card word, `waiting_reason`, and the time since `last_activity_ms`; the excerpt is a follow-up. The same commit corrects line 207 to say the excerpt is not on the port yet.
- **"Revoked" cannot be said by the host.** Revoke deletes the `PairedDevice` (`src/core/remote.rs:86–92`), so a revoked token and an unknown one are the same 401 `unauthorized` (`src/app.rs:3142–3149`; Settled, tree bullet on 401). The page infers it from `/info`, which it can read unauthenticated: a 401 with the stored `server_id` and `spki_sha256` unchanged says "this device was removed on the host; pair again"; a different key or id says "identity changed, pair again"; no answer says "can't reach the host". No host change, and no new error code that could not be told the truth.
- **The events socket is an enhancement, not the base.** The issue has the page open `/api/v1/events` directly and meets "moves to the top without a reload" with it. Safari does not support `wss://` to a self-signed certificate even when trusted (Settled, "Certificate trust"), and a failed handshake exposes only close code 1006 (Settled, "WebSocket in browsers"). The base is polling the same REST routes, applying replies by revision as §4.4 says; the socket, when it connects, makes a change arrive at once. Acceptance steps 2 and 3 are met by polling on every browser.
- **The device cannot read its own scope back, so the issue's "hidden when the device lacks `control`" needs one small route.** `scope` in `/info` is the listing parameter, not a device property, and the tree has no `/me` (`src/app.rs:3027–3031`, `3044–3116`). The plan adds `GET /api/v1/me`.
- **The QR names an address the port may not answer on.** `src/ui/remote.rs:157–164` takes `local_address()` whatever `listen.lan` says. The URL uses it only when the port listens on the network, and `127.0.0.1` otherwise, with a line in the window saying the port is Mac-only.
- **Pre-pairing surface.** `docs/remote-client.md:306` and `:319` (and §4.3, line 194) give `/info` and `/pair`. It becomes those two and the three page paths; the plan amends them.

## The record

No record changes. `SCHEMA_VERSION` (16, `src/core/model.rs:12`), `VIEWS_SCHEMA_VERSION` (7, `model.rs:612`) and `IDENTITY_SCHEMA_VERSION` (1, `src/ports/remote.rs:17`) do not move. `devices.json` gains no field: a browser is a `PairedDevice` whose `name` is the body's `device_name` (`src/app.rs:3650–3655`, capped at 64 in `src/core/remote.rs:169`), which the page sets from its user agent ("Safari on iPhone"); its scope is the pairing window's. The page keeps nothing the host needs; the browser keeps the token in an `HttpOnly` cookie and, in `localStorage`, only `{server_id, spki_sha256, server_name}`, which is public and is what lets a later 401 be told from a changed key.

One existing field changes value. **`identity.json`'s `certificate` is reissued over the same key with IP subject alternative names** (the address in the URL and `127.0.0.1`). The certificate has none today (`remote.rs:101–106`), and Chrome matches names only against the SAN (Settled, "Certificate trust"), so the page must not rely on the click-through being offered. The pin is of the key, so every native pin holds. The reissue is persisted rather than made at each launch because a browser's exception is per certificate, and ECDSA signing is randomised, so a certificate remade at each launch would put the warning back at each launch. This is a new value for an existing field, not a new field: no bump. It is reissued once for an installation whose stored certificate has no SAN, and again only when the wanted address set is not covered.

The pairing window stays in memory and unsaved (`src/core/remote.rs:46–54`). The page's rehydration after a restart is a request: `/me` with the cookie.

## The signals

None new. The waiting mark is `SessionView.waiting` and `waiting_reason`; "moves to the top" is the revision in every envelope changing (`src/app.rs:3730–3741`) or a `changed` frame (§4.4). The host emits nothing the headset does not already receive.

## The actions and effects

**Host transport (`src/adapters/remote.rs`, `src/app.rs`).**

- **Cookie.** `/pair` takes an optional `"transport": "cookie"` in its body (additive; a native client omits it). With it, the reply carries `Set-Cookie: __Host-sb=<token>; Max-Age=34560000; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict` and the body **omits `token`**, so the page's script never holds it. Without it, the reply is unchanged. `read_request` takes `cookie`, `origin` and `host` into new `RemoteRequest` fields; the struct literal is at `remote.rs:506` only (Settled, tree bullet 1). `authenticate` (`app.rs:3127`) uses the bearer if present, else the `__Host-sb` value.
  - Where the credential lives is the security decision, so this is the safer store: a cookie the page's script cannot read, not `localStorage`, and not a `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` value. Settled gives the mechanics for the socket (cookies ride the handshake, credentials mode `include`); whether Safari and Chrome store and send a `Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict` cookie set from a user-accepted certificate on an IP-literal host is **Unresolved 3**. It is the first thing the implementer tests (see Order of work). If it fails in a browser, the fallback is a follow-up for the owner (below), not a second transport built now.
  - **Limits, stated.** A cookie is not scoped by port, so another HTTPS service the owner runs on the same address receives it. `__Host-` fixes the host and path, not the port. The cookie name is a prefix the browser enforces (`Secure`, `Path=/`, no `Domain`).
  - **Cross-site writes.** A request authenticated by cookie alone must, if it is not a `GET`, or is an upgrade, carry `Origin: https://<Host header>`; otherwise 403, code `origin`. A bearer request is exempt (native clients send no `Origin`). `SameSite=Strict` already withholds the cookie cross-site; this closes the same-site, other-port case.
- **Reply headers.** `RemoteReply` (`remote.rs:388`) gains `headers: Vec<(&'static str, String)>`, written by `respond` (`remote.rs:530`). There are about twenty literals in `src/app.rs` plus the one in `connection` (Settled, tree bullet 1): add `RemoteReply::new(status, body, authenticated)` and convert them mechanically, so the one site that sets a header says so. `respond` also adds `Cache-Control: no-store` and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` to every JSON reply, which no client reads.
- **`GET /api/v1/me`**, read scope, answers `{device_id, name, scope, server_id, server_name}` from the authenticated device and the identity. It is not in `capabilities`: no Swift client calls it.

**Pages, answered on the connection thread.** `GET /`, `GET /app.js` and `GET /app.css`, matched exactly, are answered in `connection` (`remote.rs:770`) from a new `src/adapters/web.rs` that holds the table of path, `Content-Type` and `include_str!` body. They never reach the frame: the bytes are constant, a page load must not wait on a busy frame, and the `DRAIN_PER_PASS` bound (`remote.rs:580`) is for work the core does. Anything else outside `/api/v1/` still reaches the frame and gets today's JSON 404 (`app.rs:3023`), `/favicon.ico` included; `index.html` declares `<link rel="icon" href="data:,">` so a browser has no reason to ask. A query on a page path is ignored and never logged (the connection thread logs nothing of a request).

- Headers on every page reply: `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; script-src 'self'; style-src 'self'; connect-src 'self'; img-src 'self' data:; base-uri 'none'; form-action 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'`, `Cache-Control: no-store`, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`, and `Connection: close`. No inline script, no inline style, no external resource. If a browser does not admit `wss:` under `connect-src 'self'`, the socket is what is lost and polling carries; that is the enhancement stance, not a gap in the base.
- **Pool and window.** A page request is an unauthenticated connection: it counts in the 4-connection pool from accept (`remote.rs:701–706`), and `Connection: close` frees the slot at once instead of holding it for the 30 s idle timeout (`remote.rs:573`). That choice does not wait on the browser's connection count (Unresolved 6); the implementer measures five parallel connections against the harness and records it in the spike. A new `Limits.page` window allows 120 page requests a minute per listener, 429 past it (a load is three; `/pair` stays at 6 and `/info` at 60, `remote.rs:583–587`). The existing pool and rate tests count `/pair` and `/info` only, so they are undisturbed; `stalled_strangers_fill_their_own_pool…` (`tests/remote.rs:3226`) is the one extended.
- **What the page shows with no fragment and no token:** a "Not paired" screen that says to open the pairing window on the Mac and scan its code, with no host name. Its one request is `/me`, answered 401.

**Certificate.** `remote::issue_certificate(key_pem, server_id, &[IpAddr])` makes a certificate over the stored key with `SanType::IpAddress` entries (rcgen, `remote.rs:101` shows the call it replaces), and `certificate_ip_names(der)` reads the entries back with the module's own `der_element` (`remote.rs:~280`). `bind_remote` (`app.rs:~2940`) already holds the key; before `tls_config` it computes the wanted set (`127.0.0.1`, plus `local_address()` when `listen.lan`), and if the stored certificate does not cover it, issues, saves through `services.remote.save_identity`, and dispatches `AppAction::CertificateReissued(String)`. The core only mirrors the field, as `IdentityLoaded` does after the app has saved, and emits no `SaveIdentity`: an emitted one would reach the rebind test in `run_remote_effect` while `remote_bound` is still `None` and bind twice. Without the mirror, the next `SetServerName` would write the old certificate back over the new one. An address change after launch is picked up at the next relisten or launch, and the dialog says so.

Whether the device then trusts it, and whether that fixes `wss://` on iOS, is Unresolved 2; the plan promises neither, and the polling base does not need it. The file is public (it is what TLS presents).

## The UI

The page (`web/`), one screen at a time, plain DOM with `textContent` only (no `innerHTML`, which keeps agent output from becoming markup):

- **Boot.** Read `location.hash`; if it holds `code`, `key` and `id`, call `history.replaceState(null, '', location.pathname)` first, hold the values in memory, `GET /api/v1/info`, and compare `spki_sha256` and `server_id` with the URL's. Mismatch: "This address is a different Switchboard than the code was for", nothing sent. Match: `POST /api/v1/pair {code, spki_sha256, device_name, transport: "cookie"}`; on success store `{server_id, spki_sha256, server_name}` and go to the list. Errors by `error.code`: `pairing_closed`, `wrong_code`, `wrong_key`, `rate_limited` each have a sentence.
- **No fragment.** `GET /api/v1/me`. 200: the list. 401: the inference from `/info` described above, or "Not paired" when nothing is stored.
- **Header.** Host name and the device's scope word, from `/me`.
- **List.** `/projects`, then `/projects/{id}/sessions` each, grouped by project, a project with a waiting session first, waiting sessions first within it. A waiting row says "Waiting on you" and `waiting_reason` in words (not colour alone), then name, kind, card word, time since `last_activity_ms`.
- **Session.** A Claude Code session (`kind: claude`) shows `/sessions/{id}/last-response`; any other kind shows `/sessions/{id}/screen`. The reply box shows when `/me` says `control` and `prompt_refusal` is null; with a refusal it shows the refusal's text and no box. Send is `POST /sessions/{id}/send {op, text}` with `op` random hex (made from `getRandomValues`, which exists without a secure context), kept so a retry after a dropped reply repeats the same op and is answered from `operations.log` rather than typed twice. A 403 `scope` re-reads `/me`. "Sent" means accepted; the session's card moving is the progress, per §4.5.
- **Refresh.** Every 3 s while the tab is visible the page reads `/waiting` and compares its `epoch` and `revision` with those of the list it holds; a different one refetches the list and the open session. A reply older than the one applied is dropped (§4.4). When the socket connects (`wss://<host>/api/v1/events`, no subprotocol), a `changed` frame triggers the same refetch at once and the poll slows to 20 s; on `resync_required`, a close or an error, the page refetches, polls at 3 s again, and retries the socket after 5 s doubling to 60 s. The page sends no `watch` frames: reading a content key puts it in the watch set for a minute (§4.4, item 3), and the poll keeps it warm.
- **Every 401** from any call runs the `/info` inference.
- **Device name** from the user agent: browser (`Edg`, `Chrome`, `Firefox`, else `Safari`) "on" device (`iPhone`, `iPad` including a Macintosh UA with touch, `Android`, `Mac`, `Windows`, `Linux`), else "Browser".

The dialog (`src/ui/remote.rs`):

- The pairing section shows the QR from the URL, keeps the code, key and address lines, and adds "Reveal certificate file". When the port is Mac-only it says so in place of the address.
- A sentence beside the existing redaction one (`remote.rs:70–76`): a browser cannot pin this Mac's key; it will warn about the certificate; proceed if the address is this Mac's, or install the certificate file on the device; pair a browser only on a network you trust; the code works once. The sentence promises nothing about which browsers allow the proceed.
- Browsers appear in the devices list like any device, with the user-agent name, scope and Revoke.

# Plan: a web control surface on the remote port (#230)

The host serves a small page from the port it already has. A phone opens it from the pairing window's QR, pairs, lists the sessions with the waiting ones first, reads a session's last response or screen, and sends a reply. The page is three embedded files (`web/index.html`, `web/app.js`, `web/app.css`) with no build step and no dependency. It speaks the protocol the headset speaks.

Yardstick for the world outside this tree: `facts.md` for #230. Where a decision rests on a line under Settled, the line is cited. Where it rests on a line under Unresolved or For the owner, the decision says so, and the default is the design that works whichever way the answer goes. Line numbers are from this worktree at `7fe8949`.

## Where this departs from the issue

- **The code travels in the URL fragment, not the query.** The issue's `/?code=…&key=…&id=…` puts the code in the request line of the first `GET`, so a server the owner has not verified receives it before any script runs, and `read_request` hands the query to the frame (`src/adapters/remote.rs:495–503`). A fragment is not part of the request target and is never sent (Settled, "Fragment and query"; RFC 9110 §4.2.5). The URL is `https://<address>:<port>/#code=<code>&key=<spki_sha256>&id=<server_id>`. The page still calls `history.replaceState` before anything else; whether Safari keeps the full URL in an earlier history entry is Unresolved 4, so the code's single use does the rest: `Paired` closes the window (`src/core/remote.rs:65`), and a leaked URL is inert after the first pairing.
- **The key in the URL is not authentication in a browser.** The issue says the comparison lets a genuine page refuse to send the code to a host whose `/info` key differs. A browser cannot see which certificate it is talking to, so a relay that terminates TLS and forwards to the real host shows the page the real key and the comparison passes. The plan keeps the comparison (it catches a QR for another host, and a stale one) and says in the dialog that it is not a defence. A browser pairing is weaker than a native one, which pins the key out of band; the dialog says "pair a browser only on a network you trust".
- **The one-line excerpt is not on the wire, and the spec says it is.** `docs/remote-client.md:207` says the card's excerpt is `last_message` from the `Stop` hook "on the record". `src/core/events.rs:127–135` stores only `last_stop_at` and `pending_at_stop`; `SessionView` (`control/src/lib.rs:637–689`) has no excerpt; the Mac computes it in the UI from the transcript (`src/ui/cards.rs:176–185`, `558–575`). Storing it would change `SessionRecord` (`src/core/model.rs:1053`, `SCHEMA_VERSION` 16) and moving the function would be a change of its own. This cut: a row shows the name, kind, the card word, `waiting_reason`, and the time since `last_activity_ms`; the excerpt is a follow-up. The same commit corrects line 207 to say the excerpt is not on the port yet.
- **"Revoked" cannot be said by the host.** Revoke deletes the `PairedDevice` (`src/core/remote.rs:86–92`), so a revoked token and an unknown one are the same 401 `unauthorized` (`src/app.rs:3142–3149`; Settled, tree bullet on 401). The page infers it from `/info`, which it can read unauthenticated: a 401 with the stored `server_id` and `spki_sha256` unchanged says "this device was removed on the host; pair again"; a different key or id says "identity changed, pair again"; no answer says "can't reach the host". No host change, and no new error code that could not be told the truth.
- **The events socket is an enhancement, not the base.** The issue has the page open `/api/v1/events` directly and meets "moves to the top without a reload" with it. Safari does not support `wss://` to a self-signed certificate even when trusted (Settled, "Certificate trust"), and a failed handshake exposes only close code 1006 (Settled, "WebSocket in browsers"). The base is polling the same REST routes, applying replies by revision as §4.4 says; the socket, when it connects, makes a change arrive at once. Acceptance steps 2 and 3 are met by polling on every browser.
- **The device cannot read its own scope back, so the issue's "hidden when the device lacks `control`" needs one small route.** `scope` in `/info` is the listing parameter, not a device property, and the tree has no `/me` (`src/app.rs:3027–3031`, `3044–3116`). The plan adds `GET /api/v1/me`.
- **The QR names an address the port may not answer on.** `src/ui/remote.rs:157–164` takes `local_address()` whatever `listen.lan` says. The URL uses it only when the port listens on the network, and `127.0.0.1` otherwise, with a line in the window saying the port is Mac-only.
- **Pre-pairing surface.** `docs/remote-client.md:306` and `:319` (and §4.3, line 194) give `/info` and `/pair`. It becomes those two and the three page paths; the plan amends them.

## The record

No record changes. `SCHEMA_VERSION` (16, `src/core/model.rs:12`), `VIEWS_SCHEMA_VERSION` (7, `model.rs:612`) and `IDENTITY_SCHEMA_VERSION` (1, `src/ports/remote.rs:17`) do not move. `devices.json` gains no field: a browser is a `PairedDevice` whose `name` is the body's `device_name` (`src/app.rs:3650–3655`, capped at 64 in `src/core/remote.rs:169`), which the page sets from its user agent ("Safari on iPhone"); its scope is the pairing window's. The page keeps nothing the host needs; the browser keeps the token in an `HttpOnly` cookie and, in `localStorage`, only `{server_id, spki_sha256, server_name}`, which is public and is what lets a later 401 be told from a changed key.

One existing field changes value. **`identity.json`'s `certificate` is reissued over the same key with IP subject alternative names** (the address in the URL and `127.0.0.1`). The certificate has none today (`remote.rs:101–106`), and Chrome matches names only against the SAN (Settled, "Certificate trust"), so the page must not rely on the click-through being offered. The pin is of the key, so every native pin holds. The reissue is persisted rather than made at each launch because a browser's exception is per certificate, and ECDSA signing is randomised, so a certificate remade at each launch would put the warning back at each launch. This is a new value for an existing field, not a new field: no bump. It is reissued once for an installation whose stored certificate has no SAN, and again only when the wanted address set is not covered.

The pairing window stays in memory and unsaved (`src/core/remote.rs:46–54`). The page's rehydration after a restart is a request: `/me` with the cookie.

None new. The waiting mark is `SessionView.waiting` and `waiting_reason`; "moves to the top" is the revision in every envelope changing (`src/app.rs:3730–3741`) or a `changed` frame (§4.4). The host emits nothing the headset does not already receive.

# Plan: a web control surface on the remote port (#230)

The host serves a small page from the port it already has. A phone opens it from the pairing window's QR, pairs, lists the sessions with the waiting ones first, reads a session's last response or screen, and sends a reply. The page is three embedded files (`web/index.html`, `web/app.js`, `web/app.css`) with no build step and no dependency. It speaks the protocol the headset speaks.

Yardstick for the world outside this tree: `facts.md` for #230. Where a decision rests on a line under Settled, the line is cited. Where it rests on a line under Unresolved or For the owner, the decision says so, and the default is the design that works whichever way the answer goes. Line numbers are from this worktree at `7fe8949`.

## Where this departs from the issue

- **The code travels in the URL fragment, not the query.** The issue's `/?code=…&key=…&id=…` puts the code in the request line of the first `GET`, so a server the owner has not verified receives it before any script runs, and `read_request` hands the query to the frame (`src/adapters/remote.rs:495–503`). A fragment is not part of the request target and is never sent (Settled, "Fragment and query"; RFC 9110 §4.2.5). The URL is `https://<address>:<port>/#code=<code>&key=<spki_sha256>&id=<server_id>`. The page still calls `history.replaceState` before anything else; whether Safari keeps the full URL in an earlier history entry is Unresolved 4, so the code's single use does the rest: `Paired` closes the window (`src/core/remote.rs:65`), and a leaked URL is inert after the first pairing.
- **The key in the URL is not authentication in a browser.** The issue says the comparison lets a genuine page refuse to send the code to a host whose `/info` key differs. A browser cannot see which certificate it is talking to, so a relay that terminates TLS and forwards to the real host shows the page the real key and the comparison passes. The plan keeps the comparison (it catches a QR for another host, and a stale one) and says in the dialog that it is not a defence. A browser pairing is weaker than a native one, which pins the key out of band; the dialog says "pair a browser only on a network you trust".
- **The one-line excerpt is not on the wire, and the spec says it is.** `docs/remote-client.md:207` says the card's excerpt is `last_message` from the `Stop` hook "on the record". `src/core/events.rs:127–135` stores only `last_stop_at` and `pending_at_stop`; `SessionView` (`control/src/lib.rs:637–689`) has no excerpt; the Mac computes it in the UI from the transcript (`src/ui/cards.rs:176–185`, `558–575`). Storing it would change `SessionRecord` (`src/core/model.rs:1053`, `SCHEMA_VERSION` 16) and moving the function would be a change of its own. This cut: a row shows the name, kind, the card word, `waiting_reason`, and the time since `last_activity_ms`; the excerpt is a follow-up. The same commit corrects line 207 to say the excerpt is not on the port yet.
- **"Revoked" cannot be said by the host.** Revoke deletes the `PairedDevice` (`src/core/remote.rs:86–92`), so a revoked token and an unknown one are the same 401 `unauthorized` (`src/app.rs:3142–3149`; Settled, tree bullet on 401). The page infers it from `/info`, which it can read unauthenticated: a 401 with the stored `server_id` and `spki_sha256` unchanged says "this device was removed on the host; pair again"; a different key or id says "identity changed, pair again"; no answer says "can't reach the host". No host change, and no new error code that could not be told the truth.
- **The events socket is an enhancement, not the base.** The issue has the page open `/api/v1/events` directly and meets "moves to the top without a reload" with it. Safari does not support `wss://` to a self-signed certificate even when trusted (Settled, "Certificate trust"), and a failed handshake exposes only close code 1006 (Settled, "WebSocket in browsers"). The base is polling the same REST routes, applying replies by revision as §4.4 says; the socket, when it connects, makes a change arrive at once. Acceptance steps 2 and 3 are met by polling on every browser.
- **The device cannot read its own scope back, so the issue's "hidden when the device lacks `control`" needs one small route.** `scope` in `/info` is the listing parameter, not a device property, and the tree has no `/me` (`src/app.rs:3027–3031`, `3044–3116`). The plan adds `GET /api/v1/me`.

- **Pre-pairing surface.** `docs/remote-client.md:306` and `:319` (and §4.3, line 194) give `/info` and `/pair`. It becomes those two and the three page paths; the plan amends them.

No record changes. `SCHEMA_VERSION` (16, `src/core/model.rs:12`), `VIEWS_SCHEMA_VERSION` (7, `model.rs:612`) and `IDENTITY_SCHEMA_VERSION` (1, `src/ports/remote.rs:17`) do not move. `devices.json` gains no field: a browser is a `PairedDevice` whose `name` is the body's `device_name` (`src/app.rs:3650–3655`, capped at 64 in `src/core/remote.rs:169`), which the page sets from its user agent ("Safari on iPhone"); its scope is the pairing window's. The certificate has none today (`remote.rs:101–106`), and Chrome matches names only against the SAN (Settled, "Certificate trust"), so the page must not rely on the click-through being offered. The pin is of the key, so every native pin holds. The reissue is persisted rather than made at each launch because a browser's exception is per certificate, and ECDSA signing is randomised, so a certificate remade at each launch would put the warning back at each launch. This is a new value for an existing field, not a new field: no bump. It is reissued once for an installation whose stored certificate has no SAN, and again only when the wanted address set is not covered.

The pairing window stays in memory and unsaved (`src/core/remote.rs:46–54`). The page's rehydration after a restart is a request: `/me` with the cookie.

The plan is written to `/Users/sbgragent/Library/Application Support/Dispatch/tickets/d12e42c9/plan/1/repo/plan.md`. I changed nothing in the worktree and ran no code or browser, so every browser behaviour in it is untested.

It departs from the issue in eight places, listed first in the plan:

- **Fragment, not query.** The code goes in `#code=…&key=…&id=…`. A query would reach whoever answers TLS in the first request line; a fragment is never sent (the facts file settles this).
- **Key comparison.** A browser can't see which certificate it's talking to, so a relay passes the check. The plan keeps the check but says it isn't a defence.
- **No excerpt.** The one-line excerpt isn't on the wire, and `docs/remote-client.md:207` wrongly says it is. Rows show the card word, waiting reason and time since last activity instead, and the plan corrects that spec line.
- **Revoked.** The host can't tell a revoked token from an unknown one. The page infers "revoked" from `/info` instead: same key plus a 401 means removed.
- **Events socket.** Safari may never connect `wss://` to a self-signed certificate, so polling is the base. The socket only makes changes arrive sooner.
- **Scope read-back.** The page needs a small `GET /api/v1/me` to know its scope.
- **QR address.** The URL uses `127.0.0.1` when the port isn't listening on the network.
- **Pre-pairing surface.** The spec's pre-pairing surface grows from `/info` and `/pair` to those plus the three page paths.

Other choices:

- **Credential store:** the token travels in an `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Strict` `__Host-sb` cookie, with an `Origin` check on cookie-authenticated writes and upgrades.
- **Cookie test:** whether browsers store that cookie on an IP address with an accepted certificate exception is unresolved. A spike tests it first. If it fails, the fallback is a follow-up for the owner.
- **Cookie limit:** a cookie isn't scoped by port, so other HTTPS services on the same address would receive it. The plan states this.
- **Certificate:** it is reissued over the same key with IP names, so native pins hold. The reissue is saved, because a new certificate at each launch would bring the browser warning back each time.
- **Certificate file:** a "Reveal certificate file" button writes a `.cer` the owner can AirDrop, for a browser that offers no way past the warning. A download from the same address would hit the same warning.
- **Page paths and limits:** the three page paths are answered on the connection thread with `Connection: close`, a strict CSP and a 120-per-minute window. They count in the 4-connection unauthenticated pool.
- **Schema:** no schema version moves, and `identity.json` only gets a new certificate value.

The plan also covers the UI, tests, order of work, docs and a one-line commit message. It ends with the contract additions to copy into the commit and the follow-ups left for the owner: the fallback if the cookie test fails, a local CA so an address change doesn't invalidate a downloaded certificate, and the excerpt on the wire.
